Improved Lower Bounds for QAC0

Malvika Raj Joshi ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: malvika@berkeley.edu. Supported by NSF grant 2311733 and DOE grant DE-SC0024124.    Avishay Tal ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: atal@berkeley.edu. Supported by an NSF CAREER Award CCF-2145474.    Francisca Vasconcelos ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: francisca@berkeley.edu. Supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, under Award No. DE-SC0024124 and the Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans.    John Wright ††thanks: University of California at Berkeley. Email: jswright@berkeley.edu. Supported by an NSF CAREER Award CCF-233971.
Abstract

In this work, we establish the strongest known lower bounds against QAC0, while allowing its full power of polynomially many ancillae and gates. Our two main results show that:

  1. 1.

    Depth 33 QAC0 circuits cannot compute PARITY regardless of size, and require at least Ω⁡(exp⁡(n))\Omega(\exp(\sqrt{n})) many gates to compute MAJORITY.

  2. 2.

    Depth 22 circuits cannot approximate high-influence Boolean functions (e.g., PARITY) with non-negligible advantage, regardless of size.

We present new techniques for simulating certain QAC0 circuits classically in AC0 to obtain our depth 33 lower bounds. In these results, we relax the output requirement of the quantum circuit to a single bit (i.e., no restrictions on input preservation/reversible computation), making our depth 22 approximation bound stronger than the previous best bound of [24]. This also enables us to draw natural comparisons with classical AC0 circuits, which can compute PARITY exactly in depth 22 using exponential size. Our proof techniques further suggest that, for boolean total functions, QAC0 circuits do not necessarily provide more power than their classical counterparts. Our third result shows that depth 22 QAC0 circuits, regardless of size, cannot exactly synthesize an nn-target nekomata state (a state whose synthesis is directly related to the computation of PARITY). This complements the depth 22 exponential size upper bound of [24] for approximating nekomata (which is used as a sub-circuit in the only known constant depth PARITY upper bound). Finally, we argue that approximating PARITY in QAC0, with at least 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) advantage on average, is just as hard as computing it exactly. Thus, extending our techniques to higher depths would also rule out approximate circuits for PARITY and related problems.

1 Introduction

In classical computation, the ability to copy information is considered an elementary operation. Every major classically studied circuit class—e.g. NC, AC, and TC—trivially contains the FAN-OUT operation. Quantumly, however, the ability to copy information is more limited and nuanced. For example, the no-cloning theorem explicitly prohibits copying quantum information. Interestingly, even the ability to copy classical information, via the quantum FAN-OUT gate, appears to offer substantial power in the quantum setting.

The relative power of the FAN-OUT operation in the classical and quantum settings has largely been formalized through the study of three circuit classes: AC0, QAC0, and QACf0{}^{0}_{f}. AC0 is the class of polynomial-sized, constant-depth circuits comprised of unlimited fan-in and  and OR operations, with NOT s allowed on the inputs and arbitrary FAN-OUT. Following the seminal works of [10, 1, 30], the celebrated work of [15] introduced the switching lemma, which proved tight exponential lower bounds on the size of bounded-depth AC0 circuits computing or even approximating PARITY. Later, [18] used this technique to establish low-degree Fourier concentration of Boolean functions implementable by AC0. Beyond profound implications for fields such as cryptography and learning theory, these results demonstrated that high-degree functions cannot be approximated by AC0. Subsequent works refined this picture: [27] proved essentially tight bounds on the Fourier spectrum of AC0, while [16] established an average-case depth hierarchy theorem, showing that increased depth strictly increases the power of AC0 even on random inputs.

In 1999, Moore proposed the QAC0 circuit class as a natural quantum analog of AC0 [19] (later published in the work of [11]). QAC0 (QACf0{}^{0}_{f}, resp.) is the class of polynomial-sized, constant-depth quantum circuits comprised of arbitrary single-qubit gates and generalized Toffoli gates (with unbounded FAN-OUT gates, resp.). Moore also posed the following fundamental question:

Is FAN-OUT ∈\in QAC0? Equivalently, is QAC0 == QACf0{}^{0}_{f}?

Note that, quantumly, FAN-OUT is equivalent to PARITY, up to Hadamard conjugation [19]. Therefore, this question can equivalently be framed as:

Is PARITY ∈\in QAC0?

Resolving this question would have several profound implications for quantum complexity and quantum computation. In the classical AC0 setting, even allowing PARITY (i.e., MOD2\texttt{MOD}_{2}) gates does not yield MODm\texttt{MOD}_{m} for general mm [23, 25]. In sharp contrast, if FAN-OUT/PARITY ∈\in QAC0, then:

  1. 1.

    QAC0 contains FAN-OUT, and thus AC0 and is substantially more powerful than AC0 [19] (PARITY ∉\notin AC0  [15]).

  2. 2.

    For any integer mm, MODm\texttt{MOD}_{m} can be implemented in QAC0 [11].

  3. 3.

    nn-qubit GHZ (cat) states can be prepared in constant depth using only single-qubit gates and a single FAN-OUT/PARITY\texttt{FAN-OUT}/\texttt{PARITY} operation [19, 17].

  4. 4.

    QAC0 can perform many powerful computations, including: majority, threshold[tt], exact[tt], counting, sorting, arithmetic, phase estimation, and the quantum Fourier transform [17].

  5. 5.

    Strong pseudo-random unitaries (PRUs) are implementable in QAC0 [9].

  6. 6.

    The quantum shallow-depth hierarchy collapses, i.e. QNCf0{}^{0}_{f} = QACf0{}^{0}_{f} =QTCf0{}^{0}_{f} and these classes can be characterized by just FAN-OUT gates and single qubit unitaries [26].

Furthermore, since QAC0 includes gates of unbounded width, standard light-cone techniques are insufficient for proving circuit lower-bounds. Thus, resolving whether PARITY ∈\in QAC0 will likely result in novel techniques for proving more general quantum circuit lower-bounds. In fact, previously-developed techniques have already led to exciting applications. For example, QAC0 Fourier concentration established by the lower-bound approach of [20] led to sample-efficient algorithms for learning single-output QAC0 channels [20, 3] and a time-efficient algorithm for average-case learning of QAC0 unitaries [28]. Additionally, the exponential-size implementation of PARITY in QAC0 proposed by [24] enabled the compression of strong QACf0{}^{0}_{f} PRUs to weak QAC0 PRUs by [9].

Despite substantial effort in proving both upper and lower-bounds [7, 22, 24, 20, 2, 8], Moore’s question has remained unresolved for nearly three decades. Prior to this work, the strongest known PARITY lower-bounds were either in the setting with limited, slightly super-linear, ancillae [2] or with unlimited ancillae, but only up to depth-22 [24, 8]. As demonstrated by the only known constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY [24], and lower-bounds against circuits with limited ancillae [20, 2], the main power of QAC0 circuits comes from their use of super-linear ancillae to generate entanglement, accounting for the lack of FAN-OUT.

In this work, we introduce novel techniques for proving QAC0 circuit lower-bounds, enabling us to give the strongest fixed-depth lower-bounds for QAC0 to-date, while still allowing its full power of polynomial ancillae. In Section 4, we prove the first depth-33 lower-bounds for QAC0, ruling out computation of exact PARITY and MAJORITY with sub-exponential size. For PARITY specifically, we further prove a size-independent depth-3 lower-bound.

In Section 5, we also prove a Fourier-tail decay bound for depth-22 QAC0 circuits with unlimited ancillae, demonstrating that they have low total influence. For these results, we treat the output of the circuit as a single bit on a designated register with no constraints on other registers. This makes our depth-22 lower bounds stronger than the previously known depth-2 approximation bound of [24] which requires the circuit to preserve the state on the input registers. This also allows us to draw analogies with classical AC0, where the output is a single bit. Interestingly, our results contrast what is known for classical circuits, since exponential-size AC0 circuits can compute PARITY exactly in depth-22.

Finally, in Section 6, we show that depth-22 QAC0 circuits cannot exactly synthesize a so-called “nekomata” state, which is closely related to FAN-OUT. For example, [24] achieves a constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY by first using an exponential-size depth-2 QAC circuit to approximately synthesize a nekomata state. We show that such a state on n=ω⁡(1)n=\omega(1) targets cannot be exactly prepared in depth-22, even with unlimited ancillae. This complements the only known O⁡(1)O(1)-depth upper-bound for approximating nekomatas, due to [24].

We present new techniques for simulating QAC0 circuits for exact computation of boolean functions in AC0. Although it is known that QAC0 (or even QNC0) provides more power than AC0 for search problems [29], and worst-case bounded error regimes for decision problems (BQAC0) [12], there are no known decision separations in which QAC0 circuit is exact. We justify our approach in Appendix A though a QAC0 reduction from exactly computing PARITY to approximating PARITY with any inverse-polylogarithmic advantage on a random input. We conclude that it is sufficient to establish lower bounds against exact QAC0 circuits for any of the problems connected to PARITY described above [11, 17, 13], to also rule out these approximate regimes.

1.1 Prior Work

We will now briefly summarize known QAC0 upper-bounds, lower-bounds, and structural results prior to this work, as listed in Table 1. We will first discuss QAC0 lower-bounds for PARITY, which can be split into two main categories: (i) restricted-ancillae and (ii) restricted-depth. We will also describe corresponding QAC0 low-degree structural results and nekomata/CAT state preparation lower-bounds. Finally, we conclude by describing the only known upper-bound for approximately computing PARITY and nekomata states in QAC0, using exponential ancillae.

Restricted-Ancillae PARITY Lower-Bounds.

The size of a QAC0 circuit is closely related to the number of ancillae it uses. By definition, the number of ancillae in QAC0 circuits is allowed to be an arbitrary polynomial in nn. The first category of PARITY lower-bounds [7, 5, 20, 2] focuses on generic depth-dd QAC0 circuits with ancillae limited to o⁡(n2)o(n^{2}). The proofs of [20, 2] follow by showing that the circuit’s Heisenberg-evolved single-qubit “output” measurement Pauli/projector can be approximated, to high precision, by low-degree objects. Beyond ruling out the computation of PARITY, these low-degree structural results enable correlation bounds against generic high-degree Boolean functions, such as MAJORITY and MODk\texttt{MOD}_{k}. The key caveat of this low-degree approach, however, is that it only holds for a depth dependent number of ancillae, which [2] pushed to slightly super-linear in nn for arbitrary constant-depth QAC0 circuits.

Restricted-Depth PARITY Lower-Bounds.

The second category of PARITY lower-bounds focuses on fixed-depth QAC circuits, without any extra constraints on the ancillae. Specifically, [24] established a depth-2 average-case approximate lower-bound, while [8] established a depth-2 worst-case exact lower-bound against PARITY ∈\in QAC0 , both with unlimited ancillae. All the known lower bounds that do not impose any restrictions on the number of ancillae beyond the default poly​(n)\text{poly}(n) fall under this category and only go up to depth-22. Both the upper and lower bounds of [24] correspond to circuits with an nn-bit output that preserve the state on the input qubits, and we refer to these circuits as “input-preserving”.

In recent work [24], Rosenthal introduced the notion of an nn-qubit “nekomata” state, of form

|Nekomata⟩=12​(|0n⟩​|ψα⟩+|1n⟩​|ψβ⟩).\displaystyle\ket{\text{Nekomata}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}+\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\beta}}\right). (1)

The nekomata is similar to |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}}, but allows for each branch to have an arbitrary ancillary state (i.e. the normalized states |ψα⟩\ket{\psi_{\alpha}} and |ψβ⟩\ket{\psi_{\beta}}). In this case, where the two branches are equally weighted (with probability 1/21/2), we refer to the state as a “balanced” nekomata.

[24] showed O⁡(1)O(1)-depth reductions between preparing nn-qubit nekomata states and computing FAN-OUT/PARITY, analogous to those for |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}}, and extended all these reductions to the approximate setting. Rosenthal also showed that any depth-dd QAC0 circuit that approximates an nn-qubit nekomata must have Ω⁡(n/(d+1))\Omega(n/(d+1)) multi-qubit gates acting on the targets.

PARITY and Nekomata Upper-Bounds.

Despite several lower-bound results for QAC0, there is only one known upper-bound for approximating PARITY in constant-depth QAC. Notably, [24] gave a depth-7 QAC circuit for approximating nn-qubit PARITY, using exp⁡(n1−o⁡(1))\exp(n^{1-o(1)}) gates (thereby requiring more resources than permitted in polynomial-sized QAC0). To achieve this, Rosenthal first gave a depth-22 circuit using an approximate nn-qubit nekomata and then used it to obtain a depth-7 circuit for approximating PARITY. Due to the recursive nature of PARITY, for any depth k=7​dk=7d, this implies QAC0 circuits of size roughly exp⁡(n1/d)\exp(n^{1/d}) approximating PARITY.

1.2 Our Results

In this work we study fixed-depth QAC circuits, specifically with depth-≤3\leq 3, and do not impose additional restrictions on ancillae. Note that for constant depth circuits, limiting the ancillae also limits the size of the circuit because each qubit can belong to at most dd gates. Our motivation for studying fixed-depth QAC circuits stems from the large gap between the only known constant-depth upper-bound for PARITY [24], which uses an exponential number of gates, and the best known techniques for arbitrary-depth circuits [7, 20, 2], which fail to rule out even O⁡(n2)O(n^{2})-sized circuits for depth-≥2\geq 2. Our main results are summarized below.

Our first result shows that depth-33 circuits (i) cannot compute MAJORITY using only sub-exponential gates and (ii) cannot compute PARITY regardless of size. The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 4 (Theorem 4.7). We note that both results apply regardless of the number of ancillae.

Theorem 1.1 (Depth-33 MAJORITY Lower-bound).

Let CC be a depth-33 QAC0 circuit CC on nn inputs with m≤2no⁡(1)m\leq 2^{n^{o(1)}} gates such that on every input 𝐱∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, CC produces the state |f⁡(𝐱)⟩t\ket{f(\bm{x})}_{t} on a designated output tt. Then, f⁡(𝐱)f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY or MAJORITY function.

Theorem 1.2 (Depth-33 PARITY Size-Independent Bound).

Let CC be a depth-33 QAC0 circuit with n>100n>100 input qubits and an arbitrary number of ancillae and gates, such that on every input 𝐱∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the circuit CC produces the state |f⁡(𝐱)⟩t\ket{f(\bm{x})}_{t} on a designated output qubit tt. Then, ff cannot be the PARITY function.

We prove these depth-33 lower-bounds in Section 4, by first showing that, after applying a quantum restriction (that keeps Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) input bits alive), the output of the remaining depth-(≤3)(\leq 3) QAC0 circuit can be simulated by a classical AC0 circuit of a slightly larger depth and size (Section 2.3.3). This immediately implies an exp⁡(nΩ⁡(1))\exp(n^{\Omega(1)})-size lower-bound due to known lower-bounds for PARITY in AC0 [15]. Our techniques also apply to other functions that behave MAJORITY giving us the first lower-bound against the MAJORITY function for QAC0 circuits with polynomial ancillae.

We observe that at very low depths (≤2\leq 2), QAC0 circuits exhibit certain monotonicity properties. For PARITY we can exploit these properties to strengthen the bound from Theorem 1.1 to a size-independent bound, Theorem 1.2, using carefully-designed classical restrictions. These restrictions rely on the property of the PARITY function being invariant under arbitrary classical restrictions, unlike MAJORITY, which requires balanced restrictions. Moreover, PARITY and MAJORITY are known to be equivalent up to a O⁡(1)O(1) factor in depth for QAC circuits [17]. Thus we expect PARITY lower bounds for higher depths to depend on the size as in Theorem 1.1.

Our second main result is a structural result for depth-2 QAC0 circuits. Namely, we show these circuits have low total influence, regardless of the number of ancillae. The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 5 (Theorem 5.1).

Theorem 1.3 (Depth-2 Influence Upper-Bound).

Let CC be a depth-2 QAC0 circuit with nn input qubits and of ancillae. Consider the function fC:{0,1}n→[0,1]f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by fC​(x)=𝐏𝐫[C accepts x]f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}]. Then, fCf_{C} has total influence O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n).

First, note that this result is tight. Specifically, consider the Tribes function TRIBES(x)=∨i=1s∧j=1wxi,j\texttt{TRIBES}(x)=\lor_{i=1}^{s}\land_{j=1}^{w}x_{i,j} that can be exactly implemented by depth-22 QAC0 circuits with s+1s+1 ancillae and has 𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[f]=Θ⁡(log⁡n){\mathbf{Inf}}[f]=\Theta(\log n) for a specific choice of parameters (s=Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)s=\Theta(n/\log n) and w=Θ⁡(log⁡n)w=\Theta(\log n)).

Theorem 1.3 follows from a proof of stronger Fourier tail bounds for functions computable by depth-2 QAC0 circuits, using novel entropy-based arguments. We also use these improved Fourier tail bounds to prove the following correlation bound against PARITY (see Corollary 5.9), thus ruling out the approximate computation of PARITY in depth-2 QAC0.

Corollary 1.4.

fCf_{C} has correlation at most exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n))\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})) with PARITY.

Our next result is a depth-2 unlimited ancillae QAC0 lower-bound against exact preparation of nekomata states. In fact, we are able to rule out a depth-22 circuit for creating any entangled state that only has nonzero amplitude in two subspaces, corresponding to the all 00s, |0→⟩[n]\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{[n]} and all 11s, |1→⟩[n]\ket{{\vec{1}}}_{[n]} branches on any set of n>1n>1 “target” qubits. We call such states, as below, “generalized nekomatas”,

|ψ⟩=α​|0n⟩​|ψα⟩+β​|1n⟩​|ψβ⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\psi}=\alpha\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\alpha}}+\beta\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\psi_{\beta}}, with ​α≠0​ and ​β≠0.\displaystyle\qquad\text{with }\alpha\neq 0\text{ and }\beta\neq 0. (2)

The informal theorem statement is as follows, with the full proof given in Section 6 (Corollary 6.1).

Theorem 1.5 (Depth-2 Nekomata Lower-Bound).

A depth-22 QAC0 circuit with an arbitrary number of ancillae and gates cannot exactly prepare a “generalized” nekomata on n>4n>4 targets.

Note that this bound is also tight, since any |n⟩\ket{{}_{n}} is also a nn-nekomata and we can construct the state |4⟩\ket{{}_{4}} in depth-22 by constructing |2⟩=|EPR⟩\ket{{}_{2}}=\ket{\mathrm{EPR}} in depth-11. Rosenthal [24] gave a circuit for approximating an nn-nekomata with exponential ancillae in depth-2, which is then used as a sub-circuit to obtain a parity circuit. Our result implies that such an approximation cannot be made exact by simply using more ancillae, thus ruling out the exact analog of Rosenthal’s parity circuit in the same depth.

Note that we define these generalized nekomata states only to aid proving our depth-22 bound against balanced nekomatas and we do not expect highly unbalanced instances to be useful or powerful. For example, the state (1−ε)⋅|0n⟩+ε⋅|1n⟩\sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)}\cdot\ket{0^{n}}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\cdot\ket{1^{n}}, which is a generalized nn-nekomata, can be simply approximated by |0n⟩\ket{0^{n}}.

Our final result provides evidence for the robustness of our exact lower-bound techniques by showing that computing PARITY approximately on a random input in QAC0 is just as hard as computing it exactly. The informal statement is as below,

Theorem 1.6 (1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)-adv for PARITY is equivalent to exact in QAC0).

Let CC be a depth-dd QAC0 circuit with nn input qubits and aa ancillae such that fC​(𝐱)f_{C}(\bm{x}), the acceptance probability of CC has correlation at least 1/log⁡(n)δ1/\log(n)^{\delta} with PARITY. Then, there exists a depth-O⁡(d)O(d) with circuit with O⁡(a⋅nδ)O(a\cdot n^{\delta}) ancillae that exactly computes PARITY on nn qubits.

We describe the main ideas behind this reduction in Section 2.6 (Theorem 2.2). The formal proof follows though a combination of several standard QAC0 techniques and we include it in appendix A.

2 Techniques

2.1 Key Challenges and High-Level Intuition

The main challenge in proving lower-bounds for QAC0 circuits stems from their ability to use multiple ancilla qubits in a single gate. In contrast, the concept of ancillae is foreign to classical AC0 circuits, as they have no advantage in using ancillae (e.g., they can be replaced with FAN-OUT).

Perhaps a more suitable classical analogue of the use of ancillae in QAC0 comes from classical reversible circuits. These circuits are significantly weaker than AC0 and limited only to use of reversible gates (i.e. TOFFOLI and NOT). They are equivalent in power to bounded-read AC0 formulae, where each variable appears at most 2d2^{d} times. In classical reversible circuits, each gate can only spread the influence of a bit to one other bit. Thus, in depth-dd we can only compute FAN-OUT of size 2d2^{d}. Therefore, depth-log⁡n\log n is necessary to perform FAN-OUT of size nn.

In the context of decision problems, a QAC0 circuit without ancillae has roughly the same power as a mere classical reversible circuit. For uniformly random inputs, the state after each layer is maximally mixed (due to unitarity and uniform input distribution). This was the key insight of [20], i.e., gates acting on many qubits are rarely active and can be removed with little error, thus enabling similar light-cone arguments to the classical reversible setting.

In QAC0 circuits with ancillae, a gate can use multiple ancillae such that all these ancillae become correlated with the input after the gate. However, even in the classical setting, there is a crucial distinction between the notions of FAN-OUT in AC0 circuits and in reversible circuits, in which a FAN-OUT operation is required to preserve reversibility. Simply being entangled with many ancillae is not an indication of the latter since the input cannot be reliably recovered from a single ancilla alone. Our techniques exploit this distinction. We observe that reversibility puts significant constraints on the type of computation that QAC0 circuits can perform. To our knowledge, these constraints cannot be bypassed with only polynomially many ancillae. To uncover the true nature of their computation, it is crucial to study these circuits without severely limiting the number of ancillae, i.e., by considering their power with an arbitrary polynomial number of ancillae.

2.2 Setup

We define the output of a QAC0 circuit to be the output on a single designated register tt, as in Section 2.2. We do not require any particular output state for qubits other than the output register tt. This is a weaker requirement than “clean-computation” or “dirty-computation” used in the prior works that establish an approximate depth-22 lower bound [24], making our results stronger. We find that, for fixed-depth circuits, relaxing the output requirement to a single register reveals more about the structure of the circuit’s computation of ff.

We say that CC computes a Boolean function f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}, if for all 𝒙∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output of C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) on tt is exactly |μf⁡(𝒙)⟩\ket{\mu_{f(\bm{x})}} and unentangled with other qubits. 2.3 Depth-3 circuits cannot compute Parity or Majority

Our proof consists of several components that we detail below.

2.3.1 Block Diagonalization of Gates

2.3.2 Quantum Analogue of Restrictions

A central building block of our depth-33 lower-bound is a new technique, referred to as the “clean-up step”. This step applies “quantum restrictions" to simplify the first layer of gates in the circuit, such that each of them depends on at most 1 input qubit. We then show that for any cleaned-up circuit of depth-≤3\leq 3, the circuit’s output can be simulated classically by a AC0 circuit whose size is polynomial in nn.

Recall that a depth-dd QAC0 circuit consists of dd layers of gates on nn input qubits, denoted by [n][n], and ancillae qubits AA with |A|=poly​(n)|A|=\text{poly}(n). The reversibility property of the circuit enforces that each qubit appears in at most one gate per layer. As evidenced by classical techniques, such as the Switching Lemma [15], it is useful to ensure that all coordinates have disjoint light-cones in the bottom layer, i.e, each layer-11 gate contains at most one input qubit. Our clean-up step lets us simply convert any QAC0 circuit computing a Boolean function ff that behaves well under restrictions (e.g., PARITY and MAJORITY) to one that computes ff on a subset of at least n/3n/3 coordinates, with the additional guarantee that each coordinate appears in at most one gate. This is reminiscent of clean-ups performed on AC0 circuits using random restrictions that simplify the first layer of gates.

As in [20], when analyzing QAC0 for approximate computation, we argue in our approximation lower bound that gates containing many input coordinates can be replaced by identity, while incurring a small error. However, this argument is not suitable for analysis of circuits with exact output, because the resultant circuit is no longer exact. In classical reversible circuits, however, this type of simplification can be achieved via deterministic restrictions, which preserve the exact computation. For instance, restricting a single coordinate of each layer-11 and gate to 00 kills the gate and leaves the rest of the coordinates unrestricted. This means that one can perform such a clean up on classical reversible circuits and leave at least half of the coordinates unrestricted (by restricting only coordinates from gates of width at least 22). However, since gates in a QAC0 circuit can be reflections about arbitrary separable states, we cannot always achieve this effect with a classical restriction.

Our technique, therefore, is a generalization of these deterministic restrictions for quantum circuits. The main idea is to restrict the input to a state lying in a subspace orthogonal to the gate’s reflection which, in effect, deactivates the gate. Additionally, we want to be able to apply these restrictions in QAC0. Finally, to ensure that the circuit still correctly outputs f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) after this quantum restriction, the restriction is specifically chosen to be a superposition of the classical restrictions that keep f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) invariant. For f=PARITYf=\texttt{PARITY} these are precisely the states formed by superpositions of classical restrictions of the same parity, and for f=MAJORITYf=\texttt{MAJORITY}, these are superpositions of classical restrictions with equal number of 00s and 11s. We describe our clean-up step as the following lemma and defer its proof to Section 4. {restatable*}[Clean-Up Lemma]lemmacleanup Let CC be a depth-dd circuit that computes f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}), where f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) is PARITY or MAJORITY, on n>2n>2 coordinates with a separable ancilla starting state. Then, there is a depth-dd circuit C′C^{\prime} that computes f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) on n/3n/3 coordinates using a separable ancilla state and satisfies that every layer-11 gate of C′C^{\prime} contains at most 11 input qubit.

It turns out that performing this clean-up step gets us most of the way to an exact depth-22 lower bound, stated below as Corollary 2.1. We note that [8] already provide a tighter bound, in terms of nn, for PARITY in depth-22. Nevertheless, we include our alternative proof of Corollary 2.1 below, which also applies to MAJORITY and encompasses the main ideas used in Section 4 for the depth-33 bound.
