2.3.3 Classical Simulation of Shallow Quantum Circuits

For our depth-33 lower bound, we show that parts of the circuit can be simulated classically in the following sense. The circuit can be described as a unitary transformation on the 2n+|A|2^{n+|A|} dimensional space of the inputs and ancillae AA. Since our ancillae start in a fixed state |0→⟩A\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A}, the state of the circuit at any point of the computation is restricted to lie in a smaller, rank 2n2^{n} subspace. Additionally, for circuits as in Section 2.2, the final state of the circuit fully lies in one of two orthogonal rank 2n−12^{n-1} subspaces, determined by the classical function of the input. Extending this idea to other circuits, for any projector Π\Pi and circuit CC, we define a classical function fC,Π:{0,1}n→{0,1}f_{C,\Pi}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} that captures whether or not C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) has a component in the +1 eigenspace of Π\Pi. We call this the activation function of Π\Pi on CC. That is,

fC,Π(𝒙)=[Π⋅C(𝒙)≠0]f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=[\Pi\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0]

where [⋅][\cdot] stands for the indicator of an event.

Observe that for any CC that exactly computes a classical function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) on a target register tt in the |μ0⟩,|μ1⟩{\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}} basis, fC,|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}) is precisely f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) and fC,|μ0⟩​⟨μ0|​(𝒙)f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}}(\bm{x}) is ¬f⁡(𝒙)\neg f(\bm{x}). However, we don’t have an analogue of this for intermediate states of the circuit. In general, it is possible for both fC,Π​(𝒙)=1f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=1 and fC,(I−Π)​(𝒙)=1f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=1, and thus fC,Π​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}) does not always provide useful information. Our key observations, enabling us to use these activation functions effectively, are as follows.

At the start of the circuit, the entire input and ancillae state lies inside the subspace 𝖲0=span⁡(|η→⟩A)⊗ℋ[n]{\mathsf{S}}_{0}=\mathrm{span}\left(\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}\right)\otimes\mathcal{H}_{[n]}, where ℋ[n]\mathcal{H}_{[n]} is the Hilbert space of our input qubits and |η→⟩A\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} is the ancillae starting state. Using the QAC0 normal form, originally proposed by [24], each gate G⁡(S)G(S) of the QAC0 circuit is a reflection about a separable state |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}. Observe that any state in the subspace 𝖲θ⟂{\mathsf{S}}_{\theta^{\perp}} that is orthogonal to |θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S} is unchanged by G⁡(S)G(S). We show that the output of shallow circuits can simulated classically by tracking the evolution of the state in only a poly​(n)\text{poly}(n) number of such subspaces through their activation functions.

Building on these insights, we describe an AC0 circuit to simulate the activation function of the projector corresponding to the singular output of cleaned-up depth-33 QAC0 circuits. Our classical simulation of depth-33 QAC0 circuits with mm ancillae produces a depth-33 poly​(m​n)\text{poly}(mn)-size AC0 circuit as stated in the theorem. {restatable*}[Depth-3 Classical Simulation]theoremacsimthm Let CC be a single-output cleaned-up depth-33 QAC0 circuit on nn inputs and mm gates that computes the function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) on nn coordinates. Then, f⁡(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(O⁡(m4⋅n4),3)f(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}),3) This is sufficient for a lower-bound against the usual setting of QAC0, which is limited to poly​(n)\text{poly}(n) gates, by applying known AC0 lower-bounds of [15]. We also present a stronger result Theorem 4.7 that rules out depth-33 QAC0 circuits for PARITY on more than O⁡(1)O(1) coordinates with unlimited number of ancillae and gates. This is based on our observation that most of the activation functions in the lower layers of the circuit are monotone in the same direction, regardless of the number of gates, which enables us to construct a deterministic (classical) restriction simplifying most of the gates. In contrast, to simplify arbitrary AC0 circuits, we need to make use of random restrictions, which introduce a dependence on the circuit size. This monotonicity property does not necessarily hold at higher depths, and we expect the lower bounds at higher depths to depend on the size.

A consequence of Section 2.3.3 is that the activation functions at lower levels of QAC0 circuits can be simplified using random restrictions on the corresponding AC0 circuits. This provides evidence of a QAC0 analog of the Switching Lemma because the simplified activation functions are either a small junta or a CNF/DNF formula. Then, for polynomial-sized QAC0 circuits, we can potentially simplify the circuit itself using additional random restrictions.

2.4 Depth-2 QAC0 Circuits have O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) Total Influence

We prove that any depth-2 QAC0 circuit CC on nn inputs has total influence O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), regardless of the number of ancillae or gates. This is established by showing exponentially small Fourier tails: for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the Fourier weight above level k=c​log⁡(1/ε)​log⁡(n/ε)k=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps) is at most ε\varepsilon, where cc is an absolute constant. Since PARITY has total influence nn, this immediately implies an average-case depth-2 lower-bound against PARITY with unlimited ancillae, as well as any Boolean function with large total influence.11 1 Furthermore, since O⁡(log⁡n)≪nO(\log n)\ll n there exists a constant nn such that any depth-22 QAC0 circuit cannot even approximately compute PARITY on nn bits.

Comparison to Prior Work – Key Challenges and New Ideas.

We compare to prior work by Nadimpalli, Parham, Vasconcelos, and Yuen [20], which shows that any depth-dd QAC0 circuit has small Fourier tails, but only for a restricted class of circuits with O⁡(n1/d)O(n^{1/d}) many ancillae. Our proof only holds in the more restricted depth-22 setting, but also in the more general unlimited ancillae setting. Nadimpalli et al. first proved their results for QAC0 circuits with no ancillae, and then applied a simple reduction to solve the case of O⁡(n1/d)O(n^{1/d}) many ancillae. We thus discuss the case of no ancillae as it is cleaner and easier to follow.

The total influence measures the average sensitivity of the circuit on a uniformly random input. On a random input, the initial state is the maximally mixed state, and since the circuit is reversible, the state is also the maximally mixed state after each layer. However, on the maximally mixed state, any CZ gate with fan-in ω⁡(log⁡n)\omega(\log n) is activated with negligible probability, and can thus be replaced by the identity gate while incurring only a small error in its Fourier tail. This leaves us with a circuit composed only of gates of fan-in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), meaning that the output depends only on a O​(log⁡n)dO(\log n)^{d} number of input qubits, and thus the total influence is at most O​(log⁡n)dO(\log n)^{d}.

This proof technique fails when we introduce ancillae since the state after each layer is no longer the maximally mixed state. For example, consider the read-once DNF circuit for the TRIBES function, where TRIBES(x)=∨i=1s∧j=1wxi,j\texttt{TRIBES}(x)=\lor_{i=1}^{s}\land_{j=1}^{w}x_{i,j} for w=Θ⁡(log⁡n)w=\Theta(\log n) and s=Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)s=\Theta(n/\log n). Note that, without loss of generality, we can apply controlled-OR and controlled- and gates (as they can be implemented using single-qubit gates before and after a CZ gate). Any read-once DNF with ss terms can be simulated by a depth-22 QAC0 circuit with s+1s+1 ancillae, where in the first layer, each of the first ss ancillae is flipped only if the corresponding term is true and in the second layer, the first ss ancillae qubits are fed into a controlled-OR gate that flips the target ancilla qubit, that will contain the value of the DNF. In the case of the TRIBES function, we get s+1=O⁡(n/log⁡n)s+1=O(n/\log n) ancillae.22 2 As this paragraph demonstrates, the TRIBES function can be implemented by depth-2 QAC0, and we see that the total influence of such circuits can be Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) as this is the total influence of the TRIBES function – proving the tightness of our total influence upper bound. Observe though that the fan-in of the second layer is O⁡(n/log⁡n)O(n/\log n), and nevertheless the gate is activated with constant probability on a uniformly random input. This is because after the first layer, the ancillae are quite “biased” towards |0⟩\ket{0}, unlike in the case of a maximally mixed state.

Clearly, fan-in is not a good indicator of which gates are active with non-negligible probability in the presence of ancillae. Håstad [15] and Linial, Mansour, and Nisan [18] that use restrictions and the switching lemma to obtain Fourier tails of constant depth circuits. Generalizing the classical proof technique to the quantum setting has remained elusive, as the proofs rely heavily on the discreteness of the classical circuits where bits are either 00 or 11 and using encoding arguments (cf. Razborov’s proof of the switching lemma in Beame’s survey [4]).

We therefore need a novel technique. We observe that the entropy of the mixed state entering a gate is a good indicator of which gates are active with non-negligible probability in the presence of ancillae, at least for the case of depth-22 circuits. Indeed, if the mixed state has a lot of entropy, and is also separable, then its “min-entropy” is large as well, which means that the state has negligible amplitude on any particular basis state. This means that the gate is activated with negligible probability. To use this approach, we need to: (i) reduce to the case of separable states entering a gate at layer 22, (ii) bound the total influence of the circuit assuming that the mixed state entering a gate has small entropy. We explain how to do this in the following. We believe that this approach can be extended to higher depths, but the main obstacle we face is that even for depth-33 circuits, the state entering a gate may not be separable, in which case it is unclear how to connect the entropy and min-entropy measures.

Proof Overview.

The proof proceeds in three main stages. First, we simplify the circuit structure by removing layer-1 gates that depend on too many input qubits. Specifically, any CZ gate at layer 1 depending on more than b=Θ⁡(log⁡(n/ε))b=\Theta(\log(n/\eps)) input qubits can be replaced with the identity gate, incurring only ε/2\varepsilon/2 error in the Fourier tail. This is because such gates are rarely active on uniformly random inputs, and their removal changes the circuit’s behavior by at most O⁡(2−b)O(2^{-b}) in ℓ2\ell_{2} distance.

Second, we apply a random-valued restriction tailored to the circuit structure. For each remaining layer-1 gate that depends on between 11 and bb input qubits, we randomly keep exactly one of its input qubits alive and fix the rest uniformly at random. Input qubits not involved in any gate remain alive. This restriction keeps alive at least n/bn/b variables and reduces the Fourier tail analysis to structured circuits where each layer-1 gate depends on at most one input qubit (but potentially many ancillae).

Third, we analyze the Fourier tails of these structured circuits. Since the computation is single-output, we focus on the single layer-2 gate gg containing the target qubit. Allowing for the ancilla starting state to be an arbitrary product state, WLOG, gg is a CZ gate that flips the phase when its input is |1m⟩\ket{1^{m}}. We partition the input qubits of gg into disjoint sets Q0,Q1,…,QnQ_{0},Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}, where QiQ_{i} contains qubits from the layer-1 gate involving input xix_{i} (if any), and Q0Q_{0} contains qubits from ancilla-only gates. On input xx, the mixed state entering gg is ρx=ρ0⊗ρ1x1⊗⋯⊗ρnxn\rho^{x}=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}^{x_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{n}^{x_{n}}, where ρib\rho_{i}^{b} is the state of QiQ_{i} when xi=bx_{i}=b, i.e., ρx\rho^{x} is a highly separable mixed state.

The analysis splits into two cases based on the activation probability of gate gg. Let ρ=𝐄x[ρx]\rho=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[\rho^{x}] be the average state over all inputs.

Case 1: If ⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩≤ε/32\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32, then gate gg is almost always inactive. In this case, replacing gg with identity changes the circuit’s acceptance probability function by at most ε/8\varepsilon/8 in ℓ2\ell_{2} distance. The resulting circuit has only one layer of gates and computes a dictator function (depends on a single input), which has zero Fourier weight above level 1. This implies that the original circuit has at most ε/4\varepsilon/4 Fourier weight above level Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log(1/\eps)).

Case 2: If ⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩≥ε/32\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\geq\varepsilon/32, i.e., the gate is activated with non-negligible probability, then most ρi0,ρi1\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1} are close to the the all 11s state. This implies that the trace distance between ρi0\rho_{i}^{0} and ρi1\rho_{i}^{1}, TD⁡(ρi0,ρi1)\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1}) is small, which implies that the influence in direction ii is small and overall the total influence is small.

To get the exponential Fourier tail bound, we express the mixed state ρ\rho as a “matrix Fourier decomposition”: First we express ρixi=ρi+(−1)xi⋅Di\rho_{i}^{x_{i}}=\rho_{i}+(-1)^{x_{i}}\cdot D_{i}, where Di=(ρi0−ρi1)/2D_{i}=(\rho_{i}^{0}-\rho_{i}^{1})/2 is the derivative with respect to xix_{i} and ρi=12​(ρi0+ρi1)\rho_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\rho_{i}^{0}+\rho_{i}^{1}) is the average state. Then, we write the Fourier decomposition of the mixed state ρx\rho^{x} as

ρx=∑R⊆[n]ρ^​(R)⋅(−1)∑i∈Rxi\rho^{x}=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}\widehat{\rho}(R)\cdot(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}

where each ρ^​(R)\widehat{\rho}(R) is expressed as a product of the ρi\rho_{i}’s (for i∉Ri\not\in R) and DiD_{i}’s (for i∈Ri\in R). This decomposition is similar to a Fourier decomposition of Boolean functions except that the coefficients ρ^​(R)\hat{\rho}(R) are density matrices. Then, we relate the Fourier coefficients of the acceptance probability function fC​(x)f_{C}(x) to those of ρx\rho^{x}. We show that for any set R⊆[n]R\subseteq[n], we have |fC^​(R)|≤‖ρ^​(R)‖1=∏i∈R‖Di‖1=∏i∈RTD⁡(ρi0,ρi1CLOSE,|\widehat{f_{C}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1},). This implies that the Fourier weight at level ℓ\ell is at most (64​ln⁡(8/ε)/ℓ)ℓ(64\ln(8/\eps)/\ell)^{\ell} using Maclaurin’s inequality. Setting ℓ=Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))\ell=\Theta(\log(1/\eps)) ensures that 𝖶≥ℓ​[fC]≤ε/4{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\ell}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon/4. Combining this with the errors from the simplification and restriction steps, we obtain the desired Fourier tail bound, which implies the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) total influence bound.

2.5 Depth-2 QAC0 Circuits Cannot Prepare Generalized Nekomatas

The proof techniques so far have focused on lower-bounds for computation of the PARITY function, which ultimately maps a variable input state into a single designated output target qubit. We will now describe our lower-bound techniques for preparation of a quantum state, which we refer to as a generalized nekomata, using a depth-2 QAC0 and unlimited ancillae.

For a QAC0 circuit synthesizing a quantum state such as a nekomatas, all qubits start in the fixed |0⟩\ket{0} state, meaning there is no input. Thus, input-based restrictions are not possible and instead we “restrict” to certain subspaces by post-selecting on the output. Furthermore, rather than just a single output qubit, there are nn target output qubits of interest. Whereas the final layer of a PARITY circuit trivially depends only on the singular gate acting on the sole output target, in a nekomata circuit O⁡(n)O(n) gates can play a non-trivial role in the final layer by acting on all nn output qubits and ancillae. Therefore, depth-2 lower bounds against nekomatas appear more challenging than those against PARITY.

Proof Sketch.

Although the state synthesis setting is fundamentally different from the input-output setting, this result follows the same core concepts behind our depth-33 bound. The proof consists of two parts.

Simplify final layer: Given a depth-dd circuit that outputs a nekomata, we construct a separable state on some subset of qubits, |η→⟩Q\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, such that, inside the eigenspace of |η→⟩​⟨η→|Q\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}, (1) the final layer is simplified (2) the state is still entangled across at least n/2n/2 of the targets, and thus still a nekomata.

Structure after a single gate: Then, we argue that such a state cannot be created by a depth-22 circuit by reasoning about the entanglement structure of states created by depth-11 circuits. Since all the qubits start in the state |0→⟩\ket{{\vec{0}}}, qubits across different gates are unentangled, and we only need to consider a single gate. We observe that the state after a single (non-trivial) gate, (I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|)⋅|0→⟩(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})\cdot\ket{{\vec{0}}}, lies in a rank 22 subspace span​{|θ→⟩,|0→⟩}\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}},\ket{{\vec{0}}}\} consisting of two non-orthogonal separable states. Additionally, for any partitioning of the qubits into targets TT and ancillae AA, it is the case that the state on TT lies in span⁡{|θ→⟩T,|0→⟩T}\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T},\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{T}\}, even when the state on AA is restricted to lie inside some subspace of ℋA\mathcal{H}_{A}. The defining property of a generalized nn-nekomata is that it has an nn-partite rank 22 Schmidt decomposition. This is not possible for a state in span​{|θ→⟩T,|0→⟩}\mathrm{span}\{\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T},\ket{{\vec{0}}}\} unless |T|=n=2|T|=n=2 because ⟨θ→T|0→⟩≠0\braket{\vec{\theta}_{T}|{\vec{0}}}\neq 0.

2.6 Exact to approximate reduction for PARITY

Recently [12] showed that the previous approximate nekomata constructions, such as [24] can be made exact using the amplitude amplification of [14] [6], thus giving a poly​(n)\text{poly}(n) size QAC0 circuit for exact PARITY/FAN-OUT/MAJORITY on 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n){\mathsf{polylog}}(n) qubits. We point out this allows us to eliminate the error in any QAC0 circuit that computes parity with at least 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) advantage on average, in the same asymptotic depth.

Theorem 2.2 (Approximate-to-Exact Parity in QAC0).

Let CC be a depth-dd QAC0 circuit with nn input qubits and aa ancillae. Consider the function fC:{0,1}n→[0,1]f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by fC​(𝐱)=𝐏𝐫[C accepts 𝐱]f_{C}(\bm{x})=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $\bm{x}$}]. Let ρ∈[−1,1]\rho\in[-1,1] be the correlation of fC​(𝐱)f_{C}(\bm{x}) with PARITY​(𝐱)\texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}), such that ρ=1/(log⁡n)δ\rho=1/(\log n)^{\delta}. Then, there is a depth-O⁡(d)O(d) circuit C′C^{\prime} using a⋅n+nO⁡(δ)a\cdot n+n^{O(\delta)} ancillae that exactly computes PARITY​(𝐱)\texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}) on every 𝐱∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

The main approximate reduction from nekomata to PARITY, [24], requires the PARITY circuit to have error on most inputs rather than on average [24]. However, this can be easily remedied by using the “poor man’s cat state” that can be constructed in QNC0 [29] to map an input 𝒙\bm{x} to a random input of the same parity as 𝒙\bm{x}. Formally, this gives us the following.

Claim 2.3 (Average-to-Worst Case PARITY).

Let CC be a depth-dd QAC0 circuit with nn input qubits and aa ancillae and define fC​(𝐱)f_{C}(\bm{x}) to be 𝐏𝐫[C accepts 𝐱]\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $\bm{x}$}]. Let γ∈[−1,1]\gamma\in[-1,1] be the correlation between fC​(𝐱)f_{C}(\bm{x}) and PARITY​(𝐱)\texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}). Then, there is a depth-d′=d+O⁡(1)d^{\prime}=d+O(1) circuit C′C^{\prime} with a′=a+O⁡(n)a^{\prime}=a+O(n) ancillae such that, for every input 𝐱∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output register of C′​(𝐱)C^{\prime}(\bm{x}) measures to |⊕𝐱⟩\ket{\oplus_{\bm{x}}} with probability ≥1/2+|γ|/2\geq 1/2+|\gamma|/2.

Then, using [24, 12] to create 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n){\mathsf{polylog}}(n) many copies of the input register, we can obtain a circuit CC with an arbitrarily low constant error. Finally, we use some standard ancilla tricks and then reflect about the state C​|+⟩⊗nC\ket{+}^{\otimes n} to obtain a nekomata.

Claim 2.4 (Approximate-to-Exact nekomata).

Let CC be a depth-dd QAC0 circuit that constructs a state on nn targets TT using aa ancillae, given by |ψ⟩T,A=C​|0a⟩\ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{a}}. Suppose that the qubits TT have ≥1/4\geq 1/4 probability of measuring to 1n1^{n} and to 0n0^{n} each, then, there exists a circuit C′C^{\prime} of depth-d′≤3​(d+2)d^{\prime}\leq 3(d+2) with a′=a+1a^{\prime}=a+1 ancillae that exactly synthesizes an nn-nekomata, i.e.

C′⋅|0a′⟩=12​|0n⟩​|φ0⟩+12​|1n⟩​|φ1⟩C^{\prime}\cdot\ket{0^{a^{\prime}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}\ket{\varphi_{0}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}\ket{\varphi_{1}}

for some states |φ0⟩,|φ1⟩\ket{\varphi_{0}},\ket{\varphi_{1}}.

We provide the formal proof of Theorem 2.2, which is a simple consequence of the aforementioned works in Appendix A. The proofs techniques we use in Section 4 and Section 6 rely on the circuit computation being exact. Nevertheless, extending these techniques to a higher depths would be sufficient to rule out approximate circuits for PARITY, MAJORITY and all related problems in QAC0.

3 Preliminaries

A depth dd 𝖰𝖠𝖢\mathsf{QAC} circuit acting on input qubits [n][n] and ancilla qubits AA consists of dd layers of multi-qubit Toffoli gates interleaved with layers of arbitrary single-qubit unitaries. The single-qubit unitaries are “free” and do not contribute to the depth. Each qubit in the circuit can appear in at most one gate per layer, and therefore the layers with multi-qubit gates are associated with a partitioning of the qubits. The inputs start in the standard basis state |𝒙⟩\ket{\bm{x}} for 𝒙∈{0,1}n\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and the ancillae start in the all |0→⟩\ket{{\vec{0}}} state.

There is an equivalent characterization of QAC0 due to [24] where all the single qubit unitaries are moved to a new layer at the end. The intermediate layers consist only of multi-qubit gates that reflect about product states and there are dd such layers. A gate GG acting on the subset of qubits SS has the form,

G⁡(S)=IS−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S,\displaystyle G(S)=I_{S}-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}, (10)

where |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} is a separable state across all of SS. Note that this gate is simply a reflection about the state |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} and is a unitary with eigenvalues ±1\pm 1. We use the vector labels such as |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} or |η→⟩S\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{S} to denote a product state on SS, whose component on any qubit q∈Sq\in S is denoted by |θq⟩\ket{\theta_{q}} or |ηq⟩\ket{\eta_{q}} respectively.

A depth dd QAC0 circuit in this normal form therefore consists of dd such layers and we assume that there are no extra single qubit unitaries in between. Additionally, we will consider single-output circuits, in which we allow the “output” to be in any basis and therefore do not need to consider the additional layer of single-qubit unitaries at the end of the computation. We define the output of such circuits as below. \qacoutput

3.1 Additional Notation

We will use the shorthand notation C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) to refer to the state C​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩AC\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}, the final state of circuit CC on input 𝒙\bm{x}, when the ancilla starting state |η→⟩A\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} is clear from the context. For a classical restriction RR, C|RC_{|R} denotes the depth ≤d\leq d QAC circuit on n−|R|n-|R| inputs given by fixing the inputs in RR and treating them as ancillae.

For a distribution DD we denote by x∼Dx\sim D a sample from the distribution. Let XX be a finite set. We denote by x∼Xx\sim X a uniformly random sample from XX.

We use the following notation while referring to the complexity of classical functions.

Definition 3.1 (AC0(s,d)(s,d)).

AC0(s,d)(s,d) refers to the set of all Boolean functions f:{0,1}n→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} computable by classical AC0 circuits of depth dd using at most ss gates.

3.2 Analysis of Boolean Functions

For every function f:{0,1}n→ℝf:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} there exists a unique Fourier representation

f⁡(x)=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)⋅(−1)∑i∈Sxif(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}{\hat{f}(S)}\cdot(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}}

where f^​(S)∈ℝ\hat{f}(S)\in{\mathbb{R}} are called the Fourier coefficients of ff. These coefficients satisfy

f^​(S)=𝐄x∼{0,1}n[f⁡(x)⋅χS​(x)]\hat{f}(S)=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}[f(x)\cdot\chi_{S}(x)]

for S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n], where χS​(x)=(−1)∑i∈Sxi\chi_{S}(x)=(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}} are the Parity functions. Indeed, one can see that the existence and uniqueness of the Fourier representation follows from the fact that the 2n2^{n} parity functions form an orthonormal basis to the space of all functions from {0,1}n{\{0,1\}}^{n} to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} equipped with inner product

⟨f,g⟩=𝐄x∼{0,1}n[f⁡(x)⋅g⁡(x)].\langle{f,g\rangle}=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[f(x)\cdot g(x)].

Parseval’s identity implies that 𝐄x∼{0,1}n[f​(x)2]=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)2\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[f(x)^{2}]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2} and both sides equal 11 if ff is a Boolean function, i.e., f:{0,1}n→{±1}f:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}.

We define the total influence of ff, 𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[f]{\mathbf{Inf}}[f], as

𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[f]=∑S⊆[n]f^​(S)2⋅|S|.{\mathbf{Inf}}[f]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2}\cdot|S|.

(In the special case where ff is a Boolean function, note that the Fourier coefficients squared of a Boolean function ff naturally define a probability distribution over the sets {S:S⊆[n]}\{S:S\subseteq[n]\} where set SS is chosen with probability f^​(S)2\hat{f}(S)^{2}. Then, the total influence is the expected size of SS under this distribution.) The total influence also equals the combinatorial quantity ∑i=1n𝐈𝐧𝐟i​[f]\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f], where 𝐈𝐧𝐟i​[f]{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f] is the influence of the ii-th coordinate on ff defined as

𝐈𝐧𝐟i​[f]=𝐄x∼{0,1}n[(|f⁡(x)−f⁡(x⊕i)|2)2]​ where ​x⊕i=(x1,…,xi−1,xi¯,xi+1,…,xn).{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f]=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}\left[\left(\tfrac{|f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})|}{2}\right)^{2}\right]\text{ where }x^{\oplus i}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1},\overline{x_{i}},x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n}).

Note that if ff is Boolean, then |f⁡(x)−f⁡(x⊕i)|2∈{0,1}\tfrac{|f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})|}{2}\in\{0,1\}, and its value indicates whether changing the ii-th coordinate in xx changes the value of ff.

We say that a coordinate ii is influential on ff if 𝐈𝐧𝐟i​[f]>0{\mathbf{Inf}}_{i}[f]>0. We say that a function is a kk-junta if at most kk of its coordinates are influential (i.e., if ff’s value depends on at most kk coordinates). In other words, ff is a kk-junta if it can be written as a function g:{0,1}k→ℝg:\{0,1\}^{k}\to{\mathbb{R}} applied to some subset of kk coordinates i1<i2<⋯<iki_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k} as follows: f⁡(x)=g⁡(xi1,xi2,…,xik)f(x)=g(x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}).

We define the Fourier weight at level kk, 𝖶k​[f]{\mathsf{W}}^{k}[f], and the Fourier tail at level kk, 𝖶≥k​[f]{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f], as

𝖶k[f]=∑S:|S|=kf^(S)2,𝖶≥k[f]=∑S:|S|≥kf^(S)2{\mathsf{W}}^{k}[f]=\sum_{S:|S|=k}\hat{f}(S)^{2},\qquad{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]=\sum_{S:|S|\geq k}\hat{f}(S)^{2}

A restriction is a partial assignment to the variables of a Boolean function. We denote it by a pair (J,z)(J,z) where J⊆[n]J\subseteq[n] is the set of coordinates that stay alive and z∈{0,1}[n]∖Jz\in\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J} is an assignment to the rest. Given a function f:{0,1}n→ℝf:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} and a restriction (J,z)(J,z), we naturally get the restricted function f|J,z:{0,1}n→ℝf|_{J,z}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}} defined by f|J,z​(x)=f​(y)f|_{J,z}(x)=f(y) where for i∈[n]i\in[n], yi=xiy_{i}=x_{i} if i∈Ji\in J and yi=ziy_{i}=z_{i} otherwise.

A random restriction is a distribution over restrictions. A random valued restriction is a distribution over restrictions of a special form – we first pick J⊆[n]J\subseteq[n] from an arbitrary distribution and then pick z∈{0,1}[n]∖Jz\in{\{0,1\}}^{[n]\setminus J} uniformly at random. The expected Fourier coefficients under random valued restrictions are well understood.

Lemma 3.2 (Fourier weights under random valued restrictions).

Let f:{0,1}n→ℝf:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}. Let JJ be a random subset of [n][n] under some arbitrary distribution DD and let z∼{0,1}[n]∖Jz\sim\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J}. Then, for any set S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n],

𝐄J,z[f|J,z^(S)2]=∑T⊆[n]f^(T)2⋅𝐏𝐫J[T∩J=S].\displaystyle\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[\widehat{f|_{J,z}}(S)^{2}]=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(T)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{J}[T\cap J=S]. (11)

In particular, for any k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}},

𝐄J,z[𝖶≥k[f|J,z]]=∑T⊆[n]f^(T)2⋅𝐏𝐫J[|T∩J|≥k].\displaystyle\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f|_{J,z}]]=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(T)^{2}\cdot\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{J}[|T\cap J|\geq k]. (12)

The proof was essentially given in [21, Prop. 4.17].

3.3 Trace Distance and its Properties

For two mixed states (density matrices) ρ,σ\rho,\sigma on the same Hilbert space, the trace distance is defined as

TD⁡(ρ,σ):=12​‖ρ−σ‖1where‖X‖1:=Tr​X†​X.\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}\qquad\text{where}\quad\|X\|_{1}:=\mathrm{Tr}\sqrt{X^{\dagger}X}.

This metric has several important properties:

  • •

    Range and equality: 0≤TD⁡(ρ,σ)≤10\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\leq 1, and TD⁡(ρ,σ)=0\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)=0 iff ρ=σ\rho=\sigma.

  • •

    Unitary invariance: TD⁡(U​ρ​U†,U​σ​U†)=TD⁡(ρ,σ)\mathrm{TD}(U\rho U^{\dagger},U\sigma U^{\dagger})=\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma) for any unitary UU.

  • •

    Tensoring: TD⁡(ρ⊗τ,σ⊗τ)=TD⁡(ρ,σ)\mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\tau,\sigma\otimes\tau)=\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma) for any fixed τ\tau.

  • •

    Triangle inequality: TD⁡(ρ,τ)≤TD⁡(ρ,σ)+TD⁡(σ,τ)\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\tau)\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)+\mathrm{TD}(\sigma,\tau).

  • •

    Contractivity under channels and measurements: Let Φ\Phi be any quantum channel. Then for all density matrices ρ,σ\rho,\sigma,

    TD⁡(Φ⁡(ρ),Φ⁡(σ))≤TD⁡(ρ,σ).\mathrm{TD}\bigl(\Phi(\rho),\,\Phi(\sigma)\bigr)\;\leq\;\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma).

    In particular, if TD⁡(ρ,σ)≤ε\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma)\leq\varepsilon, then the outputs Φ⁡(ρ)\Phi(\rho) and Φ⁡(σ)\Phi(\sigma) are also ε\varepsilon-close in trace distance. Hence no quantum operation or measurement can increase the statistical distance beyond ε\varepsilon.

3.4 Activation Functions

We will refer to activation functions of projectors on intermediate states of our circuit, described by the corresponding sub-circuit. These are defined below.

Definition 3.3 (Projector Activation Function).

Given a QAC0 circuit CC on nn inputs and any projector ΠS\Pi_{S} acting on a subset of qubits SS, the activation function of ΠS\Pi_{S} on CC is a classical Boolean function, fC,ΠS:{0,1}n→{0,1}f_{C,\Pi_{S}}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} defined as.

fC,ΠS(𝒙):=[ΠS⋅C(𝒙)≠0]f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}):=\left[\Pi_{S}\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0\right]

where the notation [⋅]\left[\cdot\right] to refers to an indicator function.

We note that it is possible for both fC,ΠS​(𝒙)=1f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x})=1 and fC,(I−ΠS)​(𝒙)=1f_{C,(I-\Pi_{S})}(\bm{x})=1, but it cannot be that both of them are 00. For a projector Π\Pi, we will use eig⁡(Π)\mathrm{eig}(\Pi) to refer to the +1+1 eigenspace of Π\Pi. Then, the activation function is essentially checking if C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) has a component in eig⁡(Π)\mathrm{eig}(\Pi).

3.4.1 Projectors and their Eigenspaces

We give some useful lemmata for manipulating projectors.

Lemma 3.4 (Projector Decomposition).

Let Π\Pi be a projector on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} that can be decomposed as Π=(⨂i=0nΠBi(i))\Pi=\left(\bigotimes_{i=0}^{n}\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\right) where BiB_{i} is a set of qubits. Then

  1. 1.

    eig⁡(Π)=⨂i=0neig⁡(ΠBi(i))\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)=\bigotimes_{i=0}^{n}\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}).

  2. 2.

    eig⁡(I−Π)=span⁡{⋃i=0neig⁡(I−ΠBi(i))}\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi)=\mathrm{span}\{\bigcup_{i=0}^{n}\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\}.

Proof.
  1. 1.

    The first item follows as any +1 eigenvector of Π\Pi is the tensor product of +1 eigenvectors for ΠBi(i)\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}.

  2. 2.

    All these projectors can be simultaneously diagonalized because they form a set of commuting observables, i.e, [(I−ΠBi(i)),(I−Π)]=0[(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}),(I-\Pi)]=0 and [(I−ΠBi(i)),(I−ΠBjj)]=0[(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}),(I-\Pi^{j}_{B_{j}})]=0 for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n]. Take any eigenvector |v⟩\ket{v} from this diagonalization. If |v⟩\ket{v} is a +1+1 eigenvector of (I−ΠBi(i))(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}) for some ii, then it is a 00 eigenvector of ΠBi(i)\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}} and Π\Pi, and thus a +1+1 eigenvector of (I−Π)(I-\Pi). If |v⟩\ket{v} is a 00 eigenvector of every (I−ΠBi(i))(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}), then from (1), it must be a +1+1 eigenvector of Π\Pi, and thus a 00 eigenvector of (I−Π)(I-\Pi).

∎

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose eig(Π)=span{⋃i∈Ieig(Π(i)}))\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)=\mathrm{span}\{\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}\})) for some set of projectors Π(i)\Pi^{(i)}. Then, any state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} that has a component inside eig⁡(Π)\mathrm{eig}(\Pi) must have a component inside one of the subspaces eig⁡(Π(i))\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}), and vice versa, i.e., Π​|ψ⟩≠0\Pi\ket{\psi}\neq 0 if and only if ∃i∈I\exists i\in I such that Π(i)​|ψ⟩≠0\Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}\neq 0.

Proof.

In one direction, suppose that Π(i)​|ψ⟩≠0\Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}\neq 0 for some ii. Then, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} has a non-zero inner product with a +1 eigenvector of Π(i)\Pi^{(i)} which is also an +1 eigenvector of Π\Pi, so we get that Π​|ψ⟩≠0\Pi\ket{\psi}\neq 0.

In the other direction, if Π(i)​|ψ⟩=0\Pi^{(i)}\ket{\psi}=0 for all ii, then |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is orthogonal to eig⁡(Π(i))\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{(i)}) for all ii and it must be orthogonal to their span, which is eig⁡(Π)\mathrm{eig}(\Pi), thus Π​|ψ⟩=0\Pi\ket{\psi}=0. ∎

3.5 Nekomata States

Definition 3.6 (Generalized nn-nekomata).

A state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is said to be a generalized nn-nekomata if, for some α≠0,β≠0\alpha\neq 0,\beta\neq 0, it has the form,

|ψ⟩=α⋅|μ1⟩t1​|μ2⟩t2​…​|μn⟩tn​|γ0⟩A+β⋅|μ1⟂⟩t1​|μ2⟂⟩t2​…​|μn⟂⟩tn​|γ1⟩A\ket{\psi}=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}

where ⟨μi|μi⟂⟩=0\braket{\mu_{i}|\mu^{\perp}_{i}}=0 for i∈[n]i\in[n]. Here AA is the set of remaining qubits referred to as the ancillae of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} and the qubits t1,t2​…​tnt_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n} are as the targets of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}.

A nekomata, as defined in the literature, has α=β=1/2\alpha=\beta=1/\sqrt{2} and |μi⟩=|0⟩\ket{\mu_{i}}=\ket{0}, and is included in the above definition.

Definition 3.7 (Generalized nekomata under separable post-selection (GNSP)).

A state |φ⟩\ket{\varphi} is said to be a generalized nn-nekomata under separable post-selection, if for some (possibly empty) subset of qubits QQ and a separable state |η→⟩Q\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, |η→⟩​⟨η→|Q⋅|φ⟩\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi} is nonzero and a (un-normalized) nn-nekomata. In other words, for some set of nn target qubits TT,

|η→⟩​⟨η→|Q⋅|φ⟩=α⋅|μ1⟩t1​|μ2⟩t2​…​|μn⟩tn​|γ0⟩A+β⋅|μ1⟂⟩t1​|μ2⟂⟩t2​…​|μn⟂⟩tn​|γ1⟩A\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\varphi}=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A}

where α≠0,β≠0\alpha\neq 0,\beta\neq 0 and ⟨μi|μi⟂⟩=0\braket{\mu_{i}|\mu^{\perp}_{i}}=0.

Then any generalized nn-nekomata is also a kk-GNSP for any k≤nk\leq n.

4 Depth-3 QAC0 Circuits Cannot Compute PARITY or MAJORITY

In this section, we will prove that depth-33 QAC0 circuits cannot compute PARITY or MAJORITY. We will first show a reduction from circuits computing PARITY or MAJORITY to circuits whose first layer is “cleaned up” in the sense that each gate depends on at most one input qubit. We will then show that any cleaned-up depth-33 QAC0 circuit cannot compute PARITY or MAJORITY. To do that, we will show that any cleaned-up depth-33 QAC0 circuit can be simulated classically in AC0.

4.1 The Clean-Up Lemma

We begin with the proof of the clean-up lemma which is restated below. \cleanup

Proof.

Note that PARITY is invariant under any classical restriction and MAJORITY is invariant under any balanced classical restriction with an equal number of 00s and 11s among the fixed coordinates. Our goal is to convert the layer-11 gates of the circuit into “cleaned up” gates that depend on at most one input qubit. We handle all the other gates as follows:

Handling Gates with exactly 2 input qubits.

Suppose that there are mm such gates, with 2​m2m total coordinates. Apply a balanced classical restriction RR on 2​⌈m/2⌉≤m+12\lceil m/2\rceil\leq m+1 coordinates, by fixing one coordinate from each gate, and potentially one extra coordinate in case mm is odd (to ensure we fix an even number of coordinates and maintain a balanced restriction). We thus restrict at most (m+1)/2​m≤2/3(m+1)/2m\leq 2/3 fraction of the coordinates. The balanced restriction ensures that the output of the resulting circuit is correct.

Handling Gates with 3 or more input qubits.

Let G⁡(S)G(S) be any such gate. We describe our quantum analogue of a restriction that turns two input qubits from S∩[n]S\cap[n] to ancillae and deactivates G⁡(S)G(S). Applying such a restriction for every gate with at least 33 input qubits deactivates all these gates, while preserving at least 1/31/3 fraction of the input qubits. Pick any two input coordinates in i,j∈S∩[n]i,j\in S\cap[n], say (i,j)=(1,2)(i,j)=(1,2) and convert them to ancilla by hard-wiring their state to |φ⟩1,2\ket{\varphi}_{1,2} satisfying (i) |φ⟩1,2:=α⋅|01⟩+β⋅|10⟩\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}:=\alpha\cdot\ket{01}+\beta\cdot\ket{10} and (ii) ⟨θ→1,2|φ⟩=0\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0. Such a state exists because the dimension of the space of states spanned by |01⟩\ket{01} and |10⟩\ket{10} is 22 and ⟨θ→1,2|φ⟩=0\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0 is a linear constraint, so there must exist a non-trivial solution. More explicitly, we choose α=a|a|2+|b|2\alpha=\frac{a}{\sqrt{|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}}} and β=−b|a|2+|b|2\beta=\frac{-b}{\sqrt{|a|^{2}+|b|^{2}}} for a=⟨θ→1,2|10⟩a=\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|10} and b=⟨θ→1,2|01⟩b=\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|01} if (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\neq(0,0) and otherwise choose α=1\alpha=1 and β=0\beta=0.

This restriction deactivates GG because ⟨θ→1,2|φ⟩=0\braket{\vec{\theta}_{1,2}|\varphi}=0. We will first argue that the output of the circuit under this restriction still computes PARITY or MAJORITY (resp.) and then reason about the resulting circuit. Let |η→⟩A\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} denote the original ancilla state, so that, on input 𝒙∈{0,1}n−2\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-2}, the resulting circuit produces the state C⋅|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩AC\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}. Also, let {|μ0⟩,|μ1⟩}\left\{\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}\right\} denote the original output basis of CC.

CC computes PARITY.

Observe that |ϕ1,2⟩\ket{\phi_{1,2}} is a superposition over two classical restrictions setting the coordinates (1,2)(1,2) to either 0101 or 1010 respectively, and that both of these restrictions flips the parity of the input. Thus, for all 𝒙\bm{x}, C⋅|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩C\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} correctly outputs PARITY according to Section 2.2 in the basis (|ν0⟩,|ν1⟩)(\ket{\nu_{0}},\ket{\nu_{1}}) for |νb⟩=|μb⊕1⟩\ket{\nu_{b}}=\ket{\mu_{b\oplus 1}} (i.e., we flip what we consider to be 00 and 11 in the output basis to accomdoate the fact that we flipped the parity of the input by restricting to |ϕ1,2⟩\ket{\phi_{1,2}}). More slowly, for b=PARITY​(𝒙)b=\texttt{PARITY}(\bm{x}), we have that

⟨μb|⋅C​|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A\displaystyle\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} =α⋅⟨μb|⋅C⋅|01​𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A+β⋅⟨μb|⋅C​|10​𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A=0.\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\cdot\ket{01\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{10\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}=0. (13)
CC computes MAJORITY.

Here, we observe that |ϕ1,2⟩\ket{\phi_{1,2}} is a superposition over two classical restrictions setting the coordinates (1,2)(1,2) to either 0101 or 1010 respectively, and that both of these restrictions maintains the majority of the input. Thus, for all 𝒙\bm{x}, C⋅|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩C\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} correctly outputs MAJORITY according to the same basis (|μ0⟩,|μ1⟩)(\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}) as before. More slowly, for b=¬MAJORITY​(𝒙)b=\neg\texttt{MAJORITY}(\bm{x}), we have that

⟨μb|⋅C​|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A\displaystyle\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} =α⋅⟨μb|⋅C⋅|01​𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A+β⋅⟨μb|⋅C​|10​𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A=0.\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\cdot\ket{01\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\bra{\mu_{b}}\cdot C\ket{10\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A}=0. (14)

So far, we have shown that the circuit’s output under this restriction still computes PARITY or MAJORITY. However, we need to implement the restriction in the standard model with separable initial ancilla state without increasing the depth of the circuit, as we explain next.

Converting back to separable ancillae.

Let DD be the depth-dd sub-circuit consisting of gates other than G⁡(S)G(S), so that, C=D⋅G⁡(S)C=D\cdot G(S). The new linear operator on the inputs is given by,

C​|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A\displaystyle C\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} =D⋅G⁡(S)​|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩A\displaystyle=D\cdot G(S)\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{A} (15)
=D⋅(I−OPEN2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|)⋅|φ⟩1,2⏟=0​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩CLOSE\displaystyle=D\cdot(I-\underbrace{2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth})\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}}_{=0}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} (16)
=D⋅|φ⟩1,2​|𝒙⟩​|η→⟩\displaystyle=D\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{1,2}\ket{\bm{x}}\ket{\vec{\eta}} (17)

Here the ancilla starting state is not necessarily separable because |φ⟩1,2\ket{\varphi}_{1,2} could be entangled. To fix this, we add a new gate G′​(t1,t2)G^{\prime}(t_{1},t_{2}) in place of GG to compute |φ⟩1,2\ket{\varphi}_{1,2} from a separable state. One such gate is given by G′=𝙲𝙽𝙾𝚃⁡(1,2)G^{\prime}=\mathtt{CNOT}(1,2) with the starting state |μ⟩1​|1⟩2\ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2}, where |μ⟩1=α​|0⟩+β​|1⟩\ket{\mu}_{1}=\alpha\ket{0}+\beta\ket{1}. Then,

G′⋅|μ⟩1​|1⟩2\displaystyle G^{\prime}\cdot\ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2} =𝙲𝙽𝙾𝚃⁡(1,2)⋅(α​|01⟩+β​|11⟩)\displaystyle=\mathtt{CNOT}(1,2)\cdot\left(\alpha\ket{01}+\beta\ket{11}\right) (18)
=α​|01⟩+β​|10⟩\displaystyle=\alpha\ket{01}+\beta\ket{10} (19)

Since the first layer in DD doesn’t apply any gate on (1,2)(1,2), the new circuit C′′=D⋅G′C^{\prime\prime}=D\cdot G^{\prime} is still a depth-≤d\leq d circuit on the other input coordinates with a separable initial ancilla state |η→⟩​|μ⟩1​|1⟩2\ket{\vec{\eta}}\ket{\mu}_{1}\ket{1}_{2}.

So far, we explained how to clean up one gate with at least 3 input qubits. Repeating this transformation for all layer-11 gates containing ≥3\geq 3 coordinates in the original circuit preserves at least 1/31/3 fraction of these coordinates.

The classical and quantum restrictions together fixes at most 2​n/32n/3 input qubits and converts them to ancillae, such that the resulting circuit acts on at least n/3n/3 coordinates and has at most one input qubit per layer-11 gate, i.e., a cleaned-up circuit. ∎

From here on, we will assume that the circuits we consider are cleaned-up. Recall that, for a QAC0 circuit CC and projector Π\Pi acting on some of its qubits, the activation function fC,Π​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}), defined in Section 3.4, checks whether C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) has a component in the non-zero eigenspace of Π\Pi (i.e., eig⁡(Π)\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)). We will show that at each layer of the circuit (which is of depth-33), the relevant activation functions can be simulated in AC0. We demonstrate this in the following sections.

4.2 AC0 Simulation of Projectors After Layer One

After the clean-up in Section 2.3.2, the state after the first layer of the circuit is separable across all input qubits, and has the following form,

C⁡(𝒙)\displaystyle C(\bm{x}) =|ψ0⟩B0⊗(⨂i∈[n]|ψi​(xi)⟩Bi)\displaystyle=\ket{\psi_{0}}_{B_{0}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i\in[n]}\ket{\psi_{i}(x_{i})}_{B_{i}}\right) (20)

where |ψi​(xi)⟩Bi\ket{\psi_{i}(x_{i})}_{B_{i}} is a state on qubits BiB_{i} in layer-11 gate containing input qubit ii, that only depends on xix_{i}, and |ψ0⟩B0\ket{\psi_{0}}_{B_{0}} is a fixed state on the remaining ancillae. In this section, we show that the activation functions of certain projectors have a simple form that lets us simulate them classically. These consist of two main building blocks: (i) projectors with few gates in their light-cones (“juntas”), described in Definition 4.1 and (ii) projectors that are separable across all the BiB_{i}’s from Equation 20. The first two lemmas show that the activation functions of these two building blocks can be simulated classically in AC0 depth-(≤2)(\leq 2).

Definition 4.1 (Junta Projector).

Given a depth-11 QAC0 circuit CC, a projector ΠS\Pi_{S} acting on a subset of qubits SS is a kk-junta projector on CC if at most kk gates in CC act on some qubit from SS.

Lemma 4.2 (Junta Projector in AC0).

Let CC be a cleaned-up depth-11 QAC0 circuit on nn inputs and ΠS\Pi_{S} be a kk-junta projector on CC. Then, fC,ΠS​(𝐱)f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}) is a kk-junta. In particular, fC,ΠS​(𝐱)f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a width kk DNF formula with at most 2k2^{k} clauses.

Proof.

Let C′C^{\prime} be the sub-circuit that only contains the gates in the light-cone of SS (i.e., the gates that contain a qubit from SS). Then, C′C^{\prime} acts on at most kk coordinates and fC,ΠS​(𝒙)=fC′,ΠS​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{\prime},\Pi_{S}}(\bm{x}). This shows that fC,ΠSf_{C,\Pi_{S}} is a kk-junta, and it is straightforward to see that any kk-junta can be written as a width kk DNF with at most 2k2^{k} clauses. (Each clause will check that the value of the kk junta variables equals a specific value for which the function should output 11.) ∎

Lemma 4.3 (Separable Projector in AC0).

Let CC be a cleaned-up depth-11 QAC0 circuit on nn inputs whose ancillae start in |0→⟩A\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A}. Let Π\Pi be projector that has the form,

Π=ΠB00⊗(⨂i=1nΠBi(i))\Pi=\Pi^{0}_{B_{0}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\right)

where BiB_{i} is the set of qubits in GiG_{i}, the layer-11 gate containing i∈[n]i\in[n] and B0⊆AB_{0}\subseteq A is the set of remaining ancillae. (note that ΠBi(i)\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}} could in particular be IBiI_{B_{i}} as this is a special case of a projector.)

Then, the following holds.

  1. 1.

    fC,Π​(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(n,1)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(n,1), and is either a constant function or given by,

    fC,Π​(𝒙)=⋀i=1nfC,ΠBi(i)​(xi)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(x_{i})
  2. 2.

    fC,(I−Π)​(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(n,1)f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(n,1), and is either the constant function or given by,

    fC,(I−Π)​(𝒙)=⋁i=1nfC,(I−ΠBi(i))​(xi).f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(x_{i}).
Proof.

First, note that for any projector ΠB0′\Pi^{\prime}_{B_{0}} acting only on the ancilla B0B_{0}, fC,ΠB0′​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi^{\prime}_{B_{0}}}(\bm{x}) is input independent. From Item (1) of Lemma 3.4, Π⋅C⁡(𝒙)≠0\Pi\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0 iff ΠBi(i)⋅C⁡(𝒙)≠0\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0 for every ii. Therefore,

fC,Π​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}) =⋀i=0nfC,ΠBi(i)​(𝒙)\displaystyle=\bigwedge_{i=0}^{n}f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(\bm{x}) (21)

and from Lemma 4.2 each fC,ΠBi(i)​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}}}(\bm{x}) for i∈[n]i\in[n] depends only on xix_{i}. Hence, this function is either 11 or given by an and gate on the variables x1,…​xnx_{1},\dots x_{n} and their negations. This completes the first part of the proof.

We continue to prove the second item. From Lemma 3.4, we have that,

eig⁡(I−Π)\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi) =span​{eig⁡((I−ΠBi(i))⊗IBi¯)}i∈{0,…,n}\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}((I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\otimes I_{\overline{B_{i}}})\right\}_{i\in\{0,\dots,n\}} (22)

Then, by Lemma 3.5, any state |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} that has a component inside eig⁡(I−Π)\mathrm{eig}(I-\Pi) must have a component inside one of the subspaces eig⁡((I−ΠBi(i))⊗IBi¯)\mathrm{eig}((I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})\otimes I_{\overline{B_{i}}}), and vice versa. This gives,

fC,(I−Π)​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x}) =⋁i=0nfC,(I−ΠBi(i))​(𝒙)\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i=0}^{n}f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(\bm{x}) (23)

and then Lemma 4.2 shows that for i∈[n]i\in[n], fC,(I−ΠBi(i))​(𝒙)f_{C,(I-\Pi^{(i)}_{B_{i}})}(\bm{x}) is depends only on the variable xix_{i}. Hence, this function is either always 11 or is given by an OR gate on the variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} or their negations.33 3 An alternative argument goes as follows: fC,(I−Π)(𝒙)=[(I−Π)⋅C(𝒙)≠0]=¬[(I−Π)⋅C(𝒙)=0]=¬[C(𝒙)∈eig(Π)]f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x})=\left[(I-\Pi)\cdot C(\bm{x})\neq 0\right]=\neg\left[(I-\Pi)\cdot C(\bm{x})=0\right]=\neg\left[C(\bm{x})\in\mathrm{eig}(\Pi)\right]. Now, for C⁡(𝒙)C(\bm{x}) to be a +1 eigenstate of Π\Pi it must be a tensor product of +1 eigenstates of ΠBi(i)\Pi_{B_{i}}^{(i)} for i∈{0,1,…,n}i\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}. Hence, the condition of C⁡(𝒙)∈eig⁡(Π)C(\bm{x})\in\mathrm{eig}(\Pi) can be rewritten as an AND function on the literals x1,¬x1​…,xn,¬xnx_{1},\neg x_{1}\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{n}, and by De Morgan’s law, fC,(I−Π)​(𝒙)f_{C,(I-\Pi)}(\bm{x}) can be written as an OR function on the same literals. ∎

Corollary 4.4 (Combinations of Separable Projectors AC0).

Let CC be a depth-11 cleaned up QAC0 circuit with ancillae in |0→⟩A\ket{{\vec{0}}}_{A} and ΠT\Pi_{T} be a projector that is given by the product of k+1k+1 projectors,

ΠT=ΠT00⊗ΠT11⊗⋯⊗ΠTkk\Pi_{T}=\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\Pi^{1}_{T_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\Pi^{k}_{T_{k}}

satisfying, ΠT00=|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|T0\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{0}} and ΠTjj=I−|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Tj\Pi^{j}_{T_{j}}=I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{j}} for j∈[k]j\in[k] for some separable states |θ→⟩T0,…,|θ→⟩Tk\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T_{0}},\ldots,\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{T_{k}}. Then, fC,ΠT​(𝐱)∈𝖠𝖢0​(O⁡(nk+1),2)f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{k+1}),2) and is a nn-DNF formula with (n+1)k(n+1)^{k} clauses.

Proof.

Let BiB_{i} be the set of qubits in the layer 11 gate containing input qubit ii and B0B_{0} be the set of remaining ancillae. For i∈[0,n],j∈[k]i\in[0,n],j\in[k], define projector 𝒬(i,j)\mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)} acting on Bi∩TjB_{i}\cap T_{j} as,

𝒬(i,j):={0if ​Bi∩Tj=∅I−|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Bi∩Tjotherwise.\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)}:=\begin{cases}0\ \ \ \text{if }B_{i}\cap T_{j}=\emptyset\\ I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{B_{i}\cap T_{j}}\ \ \ \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (24)

Then, since (I−ΠTjj)=|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Tj(I-\Pi^{j}_{T_{j}})=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{T_{j}}, we can apply Lemma 3.4 to get,

eig⁡(ΠTjj)\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{j}_{T_{j}}) =span​{eig⁡(𝒬(i,j)⊗ITj∖Bi)}i∈[0,n].\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}\left({\mathcal{Q}^{(i,j)}\otimes I_{T_{j}\setminus B_{i}}}\right)\right\}_{i\in[0,n]}. (25)

Now, for a tuple 𝒛∈[0,n]k\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}, define the following projector,

𝒫⁡(𝒛):=⨂j∈[k]𝒬(zj,j).\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}):=\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}\mathcal{Q}^{(z_{j},j)}. (26)

Combining with Equation 25 gives,

eig⁡(ΠT11⊗⋯⊗ΠTkk)\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{1}_{T_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\Pi^{k}_{T_{k}}) =span​{eig⁡(𝒫⁡(𝒛))}𝒛∈[0,n]k\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}))\right\}_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}} (27)
⇒eig⁡(ΠT)\displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathrm{eig}(\Pi_{T}) =span​{eig⁡(ΠT00⊗𝒫⁡(𝒛))}𝒛∈[0,n]k.\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}))\right\}_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}}. (28)

Therefore, from Lemma 3.5,

fC,ΠT​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x}) =⋁𝒛∈[0,n]kfC,ΠT00⊗𝒫⁡(𝒛)​(𝒙)\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{z}\in[0,n]^{k}}f_{C,\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z})}(\bm{x}) (29)

By definition 𝒫⁡(𝒛)\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}) is separable across all the BiB_{i}s for i∈[0,n]i\in[0,n] and so is ΠT00⊗𝒫⁡(𝒛)\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z}). Therefore, from Lemma 4.3, each fC,ΠT0⊗𝒫⁡(𝒛)0​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi^{0}_{T_{0}\otimes\mathcal{P}(\bm{z})}}(\bm{x}) is a width ≤n\leq n and function and taking an OR of (n+1)k(n+1)^{k} of them gives fC,Π​(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(O⁡(nk+1),2)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{k+1}),2). ∎

4.3 AC0 Simulation of Projectors After Layer Two

Consider a depth-22 circuit C=L(2)⋅L(1)C=L^{(2)}\cdot L^{(1)} whose depth-11 sub-circuit is given by L(1)L^{(1)}. A projector ΠS\Pi_{S} that is a kk junta-projector on L(1)L^{(1)} may not necessarily have a small light-cone in CC, making it challenging to simulate its activation function. In the case that ΠS\Pi_{S} is also a kk junta-projector on the depth-11 sub-circuit formed by L(2)L^{(2)}, we can break it up into the building blocks from Section 4.2 to simulate its activation function. As it turns out, this is sufficient for the purpose of simulating the output of depth-≤3\leq 3 circuits (see Section 4.4 for the proof).

Lemma 4.5 (Layer-2 Small Projector).

Let C=L(2)⋅L(1)C=L^{(2)}\cdot L^{(1)} be a cleaned up depth-22 QAC0 circuit on nn inputs and ΠT\Pi_{T} be a projector on a subset of qubits TT. Suppose that ΠT\Pi_{T} is a kk-junta projector on both the depth-11 circuits L(1)L^{(1)} and L(2)L^{(2)}, formed by the gates in layers 11 and 22 of CC respectively. Then, fC,ΠT​(𝐱)f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x}) can be written as a DNF of size at most O⁡(4k⋅nk+1)O(4^{k}\cdot n^{k+1}).

Proof.

The depth-11 sub-circuit formed by L(1)L^{(1)} can be partitioned into D1⊗D2D_{1}\otimes D_{2}, where D1D_{1} is the sub-circuit formed by ≤k\leq k layer-11 gates on TT, and D2D_{2} contains the remaining gates. Assume without loss of generality that L(2)L^{(2)} contains only the ≤k\leq k gates G1​(S1)​…​Gk​(Sk)G_{1}(S_{1})\dots G_{k}(S_{k}), in the light-cone of TT (as the remaining gates can be replaced with identity, not affecting the output of the circuit).

First, we partition each SjS_{j} into Xj,YjX_{j},Y_{j} where Xj=Sj∖TX_{j}=S_{j}\setminus T and Yj=Sj∩TY_{j}=S_{j}\cap T and define,

X:=⋃j∈[k]Xj,\displaystyle X:=\bigcup_{j\in[k]}X_{j}, (30)
Y:=⋃j∈[k]Yj\displaystyle Y:=\bigcup_{j\in[k]}Y_{j} (31)

Then, X∪TX\cup T belongs to the same set of layer-11 and layer-22 gates as TT, so we will proceed assuming without loss of generality that X⊆TX\subseteq T by extending ΠT→ΠT⊗IX∖T\Pi_{T}\to\Pi_{T}\otimes I_{X\setminus T} to act on X∪TX\cup T.

By the Heisenberg evolution of ΠT⊗IY\Pi_{T}\otimes I_{Y} acting on CC to Π^T,Y=(L(2))†​Π​L(2)\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi L^{(2)} acting on L(1)L^{(1)},

fC,Π​(𝒙)=fL(1),Π^T,Y​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x})=f_{L^{(1)},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}(\bm{x}) (32)

Hence, it is sufficient to show that fL(1),Π^T,Y∈𝖠𝖢0f_{L^{(1)},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}. We will do so by decomposing Π^T,Y\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} into the building blocks from Section 4.2.

For each Gj​(Sj)G_{j}(S_{j}), treating YjY_{j} as the controls and XjX_{j} as the targets (ref. Section 2.3.1) gives,

Gj​(Sj)\displaystyle G_{j}(S_{j}) :=(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Sj)\displaystyle:=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S_{j}}) (33)
=(I−|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Yj)⊗IXj+|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Yj⊗(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Xj)⏟Gj​(Xj)\displaystyle=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}})\otimes I_{X_{j}}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}}\otimes\underbrace{(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})}_{G_{j}(X_{j})} (34)

We will describe below the block-diagonalization of Π^T,Y=(L(2))†​Π​L(2)\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi L^{(2)} into 2k2^{k} subspaces corresponding to the subspaces of ℋY\mathcal{H}_{Y}. We will then argue that, inside each subspace, Π^T,Y\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} is separable across T,YT,Y and its component on TT is a kk-junta projector, while its component on YY has the form in Corollary 4.4. Define 𝒬Yj(1)=|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Yj\mathcal{Q}^{(1)}_{Y_{j}}=\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{Y_{j}} and 𝒬Yj(0)=I−𝒬Yj1\mathcal{Q}^{(0)}_{Y_{j}}=I-\mathcal{Q}^{1}_{Y_{j}} for each j∈[k]j\in[k]. Then, Equation 34 becomes,

Gj​(Sj)\displaystyle G_{j}(S_{j}) =𝒬Yj(0)⊗IXj+𝒬Yj(1)⊗Gj​(Xj)\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}^{(0)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes I_{X_{j}}+\mathcal{Q}^{(1)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes G_{j}(X_{j}) (35)

and for both values of b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\},

[𝒬Yj(b),Gj​(Sj)]\displaystyle[\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}},G_{j}(S_{j})] =0\displaystyle=0 (i.e., the commutator is 00.)
𝒬Yj(b)⋅Gj​(Sj)\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}}\cdot G_{j}(S_{j}) =𝒬Yj(b)⊗(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Xj)b⏟Gj​(Xj)b\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}^{(b)}_{Y_{j}}\otimes\underbrace{(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})^{b}}_{G_{j}(X_{j})^{b}} (36)

where, for a unitary UU, U0=IU^{0}=I and U1=UU^{1}=U and [O1,O2][O_{1},O_{2}] denotes the commutator of two operators O1,O2O_{1},O_{2}. Then, we identify each subspace by a kk-bit string 𝒚\bm{y}. For each 𝒚∈{0,1}k\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}, the projector onto this subspace, 𝒬​(𝒚)Y⊗IX\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}\otimes I_{X}, is given by,

𝒬​(𝒚)Y\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}({\bm{y}})_{Y} :=⨂j∈[k]𝒬Yjyj\displaystyle:=\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}\mathcal{Q}^{y_{j}}_{Y_{j}} (37)

Due to Equation 36, [𝒬⁡(𝒚),L(2)]=0[\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y}),L^{(2)}]=0. Then, L(2)L^{(2)} inside this subspace is a unitary U⁡(𝒚)U(\bm{y}) on XX given by,

𝒬⁡(𝒚)⋅L(2)\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\cdot L^{(2)} =𝒬⁡(𝒚)⊗(⨂j∈[k](I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|Xj)yj)\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{j\in[k]}(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{X_{j}})^{y_{j}}\right) (38)
=𝒬⁡(𝒚)⊗U​(𝒚)X\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})\otimes U(\bm{y})_{X} (39)

Putting it all together, we can block-diagonalize Π^T,Y\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} as,

Π^T,Y\displaystyle\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y} =(L(2))†​ΠT​L(2)\displaystyle=(L^{(2)})^{\dagger}\Pi_{T}L^{(2)} (40)
=⨁𝒚∈{0,1}kU​(𝒚)†⋅ΠT⋅U⁡(𝒚)⏟𝒫​(𝒚)T⊗𝒬​(𝒚)Y\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\underbrace{U(\bm{y})^{\dagger}\cdot\Pi_{T}\cdot U(\bm{y})}_{\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}}\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y} (41)
=⨁𝒚∈{0,1}k𝒫​(𝒚)T⊗𝒬​(𝒚)Y\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y} (42)

where each 𝒫⁡(𝒚)\mathcal{P}(\bm{y}) is a projector only on TT. Therefore,

fC,ΠT​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C,\Pi_{T}}(\bm{x}) =fD1⊗D2,Π^T,Y​(𝒙)\displaystyle=f_{D_{1}\otimes D_{2},\widehat{\Pi}_{T,Y}}(\bm{x}) (43)
=⋁𝒚∈{0,1}kfD1⊗D2,𝒫⁡(𝒚)⊗𝒬⁡(𝒚)​(𝒙)\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}f_{D_{1}\otimes D_{2},\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})\otimes\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})}(\bm{x}) (44)
=⋁𝒚∈{0,1}k(fD1,𝒫​(𝒚)T​(𝒙)​⋀fD2,𝒬​(𝒚)Y​(𝒙))\displaystyle=\bigvee_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{k}}\left(f_{D_{1},\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D_{2},\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})_{Y}}(\bm{x})\right) (45)

Since 𝒫​(𝒚)T\mathcal{P}(\bm{y})_{T} only acts on D1D_{1}, it is a kk-junta projector and can be implemented by a DNF of size at most 2k+12^{k}+1 according to Lemma 4.2. Also, from Corollary 4.4, fD2,𝒬⁡(𝒚)f_{D_{2},\mathcal{Q}(\bm{y})} can be implemented by a DNF of size at most O⁡(nk+1)O(n^{k+1}). The AND of two DNFs of size s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} can be written as a DNF of size s1⋅s2s_{1}\cdot s_{2} whose terms are all pairwise ANDs of all pairs of terms in the original DNFs. Therefore, fC,Π​(𝒙)f_{C,\Pi}(\bm{x}) can be written as a DNF of size at most O⁡(4k⋅nk+1)O(4^{k}\cdot n^{k+1}). ∎

4.4 AC0 Simulation of cleaned-up depth-3 circuits

Now we have all the pieces to prove Section 2.3.3. \acsimthm

Proof.

Suppose that CC computes a function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) with nn coordinates (for large enough nn) on register tt in the |μb⟩\ket{\mu_{b}} basis. Then, fC,|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)=f⁡(𝒙)f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}). Let G⁡(S,t)=(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S,t)G(S,t)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S,t}) be the final (layer-3) gate on tt and let DD be the depth-22 sub-circuit. Since other layer-33 gates do not affect the output on tt, without loss of generality, we can assume that C=G⋅DC=G\cdot D (i.e., there are no other layer-33 gates other than GG).

Let θS⟂=(I−|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S)\theta^{\perp}_{S}=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) and |μb~⟩=(It−2​|θt⟩​⟨θt|)⋅|μb⟩\ket{\widetilde{\mu_{b}}}=(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t})\cdot\ket{\mu_{b}} for b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. Consider the following function,

g⁡(𝒙)={fD,θS⟂⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙), if ​fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)=1fD,|μ1~⟩​⟨μ1~|​(𝒙), otherwise .\displaystyle g(\bm{x})=\begin{cases}f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}),&\text{ if }f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1\\ f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}),&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}. (46)

It is sufficient to argue that: (1) g⁡(𝒙)=fC,|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)=f⁡(𝒙)g(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f(\bm{x}) and (2) g⁡(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(O⁡(m4⋅n4),3)g(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}),3).

Proof of (1).

Recall from Section 2.3.1 that we can treat tt as the “target” and SS as the controls in GG to decompose it as:

G⁡(S,t)\displaystyle G(S,t) =θS⟂⊗It+|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S⊗(It−2​|θt⟩​⟨θt|)\displaystyle=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t}) (47)

We will show that the output of g⁡(𝒙)g(\bm{x}) is correct for each of the two cases in Equation 46 (i.e., for the case fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)=1f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1 and its complement).

The Case fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)=1f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})=1:

In this case θS⟂⋅D⁡(𝒙)≠0\theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot D(\bm{x})\neq 0. Then, there must exists a b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} such that θS⟂⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|⋅D⁡(𝒙)≠0\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot D(\bm{x})\neq 0, because |μ0⟩​⟨μ0|t+|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|t=It\outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}_{t}+\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}_{t}=I_{t}. This means that fD,θS⟂⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|​(𝒙)=1f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=1 for some b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.

On the other hand, θS⟂\theta^{\perp}_{S} deactivates GG, i.e., θS⟂⋅G=θS⟂⊗It\theta^{\perp}_{S}\cdot G=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}, and thus for any b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\},

θS⟂⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|⋅C=θS⟂⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|⋅D.\displaystyle\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot C=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}\cdot D. (48)

In particular for b=¬f⁡(𝒙)b=\neg f(\bm{x}) the LHS of the above equation equals 00 and thus fD,θS⟂⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|​(𝒙)=0f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=0. and thus in this case, f⁡(𝒙)=fC,|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)=fD,|μ1~⟩​⟨μ1~|​(𝒙)f(\bm{x})=f_{C,\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})=f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}).

By Part (1), we have that

so it suffices to show that each of the three activation functions can be implemented in AC0.

Let m1,m2m_{1},m_{2} be the number of layer 11 and 22 gates respectively and for ℓ∈[2],j∈[mℓ]\ell\in[2],j\in[m_{\ell}], let Bℓ,jB_{\ell,j} denote the set of qubits in the jjth gate at layer ℓ\ell. eig⁡(θS⟂)\displaystyle\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S}) =span​{eig⁡(θSi​j⟂⊗IS∖Si​j)}i∈[0,m1],j∈[0,m2]\displaystyle=\mathrm{span}{\left\{\mathrm{eig}(\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}}\otimes I_{S\setminus S_{ij}})\right\}}_{i\in\left[0,m_{1}\right],\ j\in\left[0,m_{2}\right]} (51)

From Lemma 3.5,

By definition θSi​j⟂\theta^{\perp}_{S_{ij}} contains qubits from at most one gate per layer. Then, due to Lemma 4.5, both these functions can be implemented by DNFs of size O⁡(n2​m2)O(n^{2}m^{2}). g⁡(𝒙)\displaystyle g(\bm{x}) =(fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)​⋀fD,θS⟂⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙))​⋁(¬fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)​⋀fD,|μ1~⟩​⟨μ1~|​(𝒙))\displaystyle=\left(f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\right)\bigvee\left(\neg f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x})\right) (55)

can be implemented as a depth-44 AC0 circuit of O⁡(m2⋅n2)O(m^{2}\cdot n^{2}) size. A slightly more careful analysis, explained next, shows that the depth is actually 33.

We show how to implement Equation 55 by an OR-AND-OR circuit of size O⁡(m4​n4)O(m^{4}n^{4}). As the AND of two DNFs of size at most O⁡(n2​m2)O(n^{2}m^{2}), the left hand side (fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)​⋀fD,θS⟂⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙))\left(f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x})\bigwedge f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\right) can be implemented as a DNF of size O⁡(m4​n4)O(m^{4}n^{4}), which is a special case of OR-AND-OR circuit.

As for the right hand side, the expression ¬fD,θS⟂​(𝒙)\neg f_{D,\theta^{\perp}_{S}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a CNF of size O⁡(n2​m2)O(n^{2}m^{2}) due to De Morgan’s law, which is an AND of O⁡(n2​m2)O(n^{2}m^{2}) clauses. Furthermore, the expression fD,|μ1~⟩​⟨μ1~|​(𝒙)f_{D,\outerproduct*{\widetilde{\mu_1}}{\widetilde{\mu_1}}}(\bm{x}) can be implemented by a DNF of size O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}).

Finally, the AND of a CNF of size s1s_{1} and a DNF of size s2s_{2} can be written as a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O⁡((s1+n)⋅s2)O((s_{1}+n)\cdot s_{2}) as follows. Suppose ϕ=C1∧⋯∧Cs1\phi=C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}} and ψ=T1∨⋯∨Ts2\psi=T_{1}\lor\dots\lor T_{s_{2}} are CNF and DNF formulas respectively where each clause CiC_{i} is an OR of literals and each term TjT_{j} is an AND of literals. Then, the AND of ϕ\phi and ψ\psi can be written as a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O⁡(s1⋅s2)O(s_{1}\cdot s_{2}) as follows.

ϕ∧ψ\displaystyle\phi\land\psi =(C1∧⋯∧Cs1)∧(T1∨⋯∨Ts2)\displaystyle=(C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}})\land(T_{1}\lor\dots\lor T_{s_{2}})
=⋁i=1s2(C1∧⋯∧Cs1∧Ti)\displaystyle=\bigvee_{i=1}^{s_{2}}(C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}}\land T_{i})

which is a OR-AND-OR circuit of size O⁡(s1⋅s2)O(s_{1}\cdot s_{2}) as (C1∧⋯∧Cs1∧Ti)(C_{1}\land\dots\land C_{s_{1}}\land T_{i}) is a CNF with at most s1+ns_{1}+n clauses as the term TiT_{i} is an AND of at most nn literals, a special case of a CNF of size nn. ∎

Corollary 4.6 (depth-3 Sub-exponential Lower Bound).

Let CC be a single-output cleaned up depth-33 QAC0 circuit CC on nn inputs with m=exp⁡(o⁡(n))m=\exp(o(\sqrt{n})) gates that computes the function f⁡(𝐱)f(\bm{x}) on nn coordinates. Then, f⁡(𝐱)f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY or MAJORITY function.

Proof.

First, we apply the clean-up step from Section 2.3.2 while keeping at least n′=n/3n^{\prime}=n/3 coordinates. Then, by Section 2.3.3, f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) is a function that can be computed by a depth-33 AC0 circuit of size O⁡(m4⋅n4)O(m^{4}\cdot n^{4}). Based on the known AC0 lower-bound of [15], if f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) is either PARITY or MAJORITY, it requires m4​n4≥exp⁡(Ω⁡(n))m^{4}n^{4}\geq\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{n})), making m≥exp⁡(Ω⁡(n))m\geq\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{n})). ∎

Theorem 4.7 (Depth-33 Lower-Bound with Unlimited Ancillae).

Let CC be a depth-33 𝖰𝖠𝖢0\mathsf{QAC}^{0} circuit on n=ω⁡(1)n=\omega(1) coordinates and an arbitrary number of ancillae and size, that computes the function f⁡(𝐱)f(\bm{x}). Then f⁡(𝐱)f(\bm{x}) cannot be the PARITY function.

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) is PARITY. First we will perform the cleanup step from Section 2.3.2, which preserves at least n/3=ω⁡(1)n/3=\omega(1) coordinates. Now we will proceed to prove the bound against cleaned up circuits on nn coordinates. To do so, we will construct a restriction that preserves Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) qubits and simplifies the final gate on the target qubit tt. From Section 2.3.1, the final gate on tt, G⁡(S,t)=(I−2​|θ→S,t⟩​⟨θ→S,t|)G(S,t)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth_{S,t}}{\vth_{S,t}}) can be viewed as a controlled-U gate on target tt as below.

G⁡(S,t)\displaystyle G(S,t) =θS⟂⊗It+|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S⊗(It−2​|θt⟩​⟨θt|)\displaystyle=\theta^{\perp}_{S}\otimes I_{t}+\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}\otimes(I_{t}-2\outerproduct*{\th_t}{\th_t}) (56)

Then, we will argue that there is a restriction to either guarantee that we are always in the θ⟂=(I−|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S)\theta^{\perp}=(I-\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) subspace, in which GG is inactive, or guarantee that we are orthogonal to the subspace, which simplifies GG into a single qubit unitary.

First we will remove all the redundant qubits from the gates, these are the qubits that are always in the state |θ⟩q\ket{\theta}_{q} regardless of the input, making |θq⟂⟩​⟨θq⟂|\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q} kill CC. Now WLOG SS contains no such qubits. We will use C2C^{2} to denote the sub-circuits consisting of gates up to layer 22.

Restrict to identity subspace.

Suppose that there is a qubit q∈Sq\in S such that |η⟩q=|θq⟂⟩\ket{\eta}_{q}=\ket{\theta^{\perp}_{q}} satisfies point (1) of Section 4.5, i.e., there exists a restriction RR on at most 2​n/32n/3 coordinates to fix fC2|R,|η⟩​⟨η|q​(𝒙)=1f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}}(\bm{x})=1. Then, C|RC|_{R} still correctly computes f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) on 𝒙∈{0,1}n−|R|\bm{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n-|R|} in some basis (|μ0⟩,|μ1⟩)\left(\ket{\mu_{0}},\ket{\mu_{1}}\right) on tt. Since |μ0⟩​⟨μ0|+|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|=I\outerproduct*{\mu_0}{\mu_0}+\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}=I, fC2|R,|η⟩​⟨η|q⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|​(𝒙)f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x}) is nonzero for some value of b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. Additionally, for b=f⁡(𝒙)⊕1b=f(\bm{x})\oplus 1, fC|R,|η⟩​⟨η|⊗|μb⟩​⟨μb|​(𝒙)=0.f_{C|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_b}{\mu_b}}(\bm{x})=0. Hence,

fC2|R,|η⟩​⟨η|⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)\displaystyle f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x}) =fC|R,|η⟩​⟨η|⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|(due to |η⟩​⟨η|⋅G=|η⟩​⟨η|⊗I)\displaystyle=f_{C|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ (\text{due to }\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\cdot G=\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}\otimes I) (57)
=f⁡(𝒙).\displaystyle=f(\bm{x}). (58)

However, from Lemma 4.5, fC2|R,|η⟩​⟨η|q⊗|μ1⟩​⟨μ1|​(𝒙)∈𝖠𝖢0​(O⁡(n3),2)f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\eta}{\eta}_{q}\otimes\outerproduct*{\mu_1}{\mu_1}}(\bm{x})\in\mathsf{AC}^{0}(O(n^{3}),2). From the known bounds of [15] for AC0 circuits, this is a contradiction to n=ω⁡(1)n=\omega(1).

No restriction to identity subspace.

This is when the previous case doesn’t apply. Let H1​…​HmH_{1}\dots H_{m} be the layer-22 gates containing at least one qubit from SS. Then, for every qubit q∈Sq\in S belonging to the layer 22 gate HjH_{j}, Section 4.5 gives that fC2,|θq⟂⟩​⟨θq⟂|​(𝒙)=fC2,Hj​(𝒙)f_{C^{2},\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}}(\bm{x})=f_{C^{2},H_{j}}(\bm{x}) and is a width ≥2​n/3\geq 2n/3 and function.

Now we will argue that there is a restriction RR on ≤0.9​n\leq 0.9n inputs, that makes fC2|R,Hj​(𝒙)=0f_{C^{2}|_{R},H_{j}}(\bm{x})=0 for all 𝒙\bm{x}. This has the effect of making fC2|R,|θq⟂⟩​⟨θq⟂|​(𝒙)=0f_{C^{2}|_{R},\outerproduct*{\pth_q}{\pth_q}}(\bm{x})=0 for all q∈Sq\in S forcing the state on SS after C2C^{2} to be |θ→⟩S\ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S} regardless of input. Then, from Equation 56, this simplifies G⁡(S,t)G(S,t) to a single qubit unitary acting only on tt, giving us a depth-≤2\leq 2 circuit computing parity on n′≥0.1​nn^{\prime}\geq 0.1n coordinates.

We will use Section 4.5 to construct RR. The idea is that the activation function corresponding to all but a O⁡(1)O(1) number of these gates is monotone in the same direction for a large fraction of the inputs. This allows us to construct a restriction that kills all these gates simultaneously while handling O⁡(1)O(1) other gates separately.
