5 Depth-2 QAC0 Circuits Have Small Total Influence

In this section, we will prove that any depth-2 QAC0 circuit has small total influence, as defined in Section 3.2. In particular, we will show that, regardless of the number of ancillae, the total influence of an nn-input depth-2 QAC0 circuit is upper-bounded by O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n). To establish this, we will prove a stronger bound on the Fourier concentration (showing exponentially small Fourier tails) of the circuit’s outcome as a function of the input qubits.

Since PARITY has total influence nn, this implies that the functions computable by depth-2 QAC0 circuits have small correlation with PARITY. Therefore, this result offers a novel average-case depth-22 lower-bound against PARITY ∈\in QAC0 with unlimited ancillae. More generally, the result implies an average-case depth-22 lower-bound against any Boolean function with large total influence.

5.1 Main Proof

We will now prove the main result of this section, showing that for any depth-22 QAC0 circuit CC, the Fourier tail of the function fC​(x)=𝐏𝐫[C accepts x]f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}] at level k=c​log⁡(1/ε)​log⁡(n/ε)k=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps) is at most ε\varepsilon, i.e. 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤ε{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon. Along the way, we will introduce several intermediate claims and lemmata that will be proved in Section 5.2. The formal theorem statement is as follows.

Theorem 5.1.

There exists a constant c≥1c\geq 1 such that the following holds. Let CC be a depth-22 QAC0 circuit with nn input qubits and any number aa of ancilla qubits. Consider the function fC:{0,1}n→[0,1]f_{C}:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to[0,1] defined by fC​(x)=𝐏𝐫[C accepts x]f_{C}(x)=\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\text{$C$ accepts $x$}]. Then, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

𝖶≥k⁡(ε)​[fC]≤ε, where ​k​(ε)=c​log⁡(1/ε)​log⁡(n/ε)\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon,\quad\textnormal{ where }\;k(\varepsilon)=c\log(1/\eps)\log(n/\eps) (64)
Proof of Theorem 5.1.

We will give an overview of the full proof with reference to several intermediate claims and lemmata. We defer the proofs of these intermediate results to Section 5.2.

We begin the proof by simplifying the CZ gates at layer 11 of the circuit, i.e., those closest to the inputs. We replace each gate that depends on many input qubits with the identity gate (incurring a small error) and then apply a random restriction tailored to the circuit structure. The purpose of these two steps is to reduce to a more structured case, where each gate at layer 11 depends on at most one input qubit (but potentially many other ancillae). Moreover, we show that these steps behave well with respect to the Fourier tails of the circuit.

Reduction to a Structured Circuit.

We consider the gates at layer 11. Recall that in QAC0, gates at a certain layer are non-overlapping. This means that for each of the layer-11 gates, g1,…,gℓg_{1},\dots,g_{\ell}, there is a set of incoming input bits, S1,…,Sℓ⊆[n]S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n], such that S1,…,SℓS_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} are disjoint (where possibly some of the SiS_{i} are empty sets, as the corresponding gates only depend on ancillae).

We first show that any gate gig_{i} whose corresponding SiS_{i} contains more than b≜log⁡(16​n/ε)b\triangleq\log(16n/\eps) inputs can be replaced with the identity gate, while incurring smalle error. In particular, Claim 5.2 shows that replacing each such gate with identity changes fCf_{C} by at most ε/2​n\varepsilon/2n in Fourier weight above level kk. Since there are at most nn such gates (because each gate depends on at least one input qubit and the gates are non-overlapping), the Fourier weight above level kk differs by at most ε/2\varepsilon/2.

Claim 5.2.

Let gg be a CZ-gate at layer 11 with input qubits S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] entering it. Let C′C^{\prime} be the circuit where gg is replaced with identity. Then ‖fC−fC′‖22≤4⋅2−|S|\|f_{C}-f_{C^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\cdot 2^{-|S|}. Furthermore, for any kk, the Fourier weight above level kk of fCf_{C} and fC′f_{C^{\prime}} differs by at most

|𝖶≥k​[fC]−𝖶≥k​[fC′]|≤8⋅2−|S|.\displaystyle|{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]-{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime}}]|\leq 8\cdot 2^{-|S|}. (65)
Random Restrictions.

We replace CC with a circuit C′C^{\prime}, replacing the above mentioned layer-11 gates that depend on more than bb input qubits with identity, and continue to analyze the Fourier tails of fC′f_{C^{\prime}}. Each layer-11 gate of fC′f_{C^{\prime}} depends on at most bb input qubits. We will apply a random-valued restriction that randomly picks at most one input qubit per gate keeping it alive and sets the remaining inputs uniformly at random. The random restriction will sample a random subset J⊆[n]J\subseteq[n] of the variables to stay alive, based on the circuit structure, and a partial assignment z∈{0,1}[n]∖Jz\in\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus J} sampled uniformly at random.

We will now describe the explicit random restriction process for sampling JJ. We consider only the gates gig_{i} for which 1≤|Si|≤b1\leq|S_{i}|\leq b (recall that b=log⁡(16​n/ε)b=\log(16n/\eps)). For each such gate, we pick exactly one of the bits in SiS_{i} to be included in JJ uniformly at random and independently of all other choices. Input qubits not involved in any gate always remain alive. Claim 5.3 demonstrates that Fourier tails behave nicely with respect to this random restriction. (Observe that this restriction always keeps at least n/bn/b variables alive.)

Claim 5.3.

Let b∈ℕb\in{\mathbb{N}} and S1,…,Sℓ⊆[n]S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n] be disjoint sets of size between 11 and bb. Define S0=[n]∖(S1∪⋯∪Sℓ)S_{0}=[n]\setminus(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{\ell}) so that S0,…,SℓS_{0},\ldots,S_{\ell} form a partition of [n][n]. Consider the random valued restriction (J,z)(J,z) that for each i∈{1,…,ℓ}i\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}, picks independently uniformly at random exactly one element from to SiS_{i} to JJ, and furthermore surely picks all elements in S0S_{0} to JJ.

Then, for any k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} and function f:{0,1}n→ℝf:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the above random restriction process satisfies

𝖶≥4​k​b​[f]≤2⋅𝐄J,z[𝖶≥k​[f|J,z]].\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq 4kb}[f]\leq 2\cdot\mathop{\bf E\/}_{J,z}[{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f|_{J,z}]]. (66)
Fourier Tail Bounds for Structured Circuits.

With Claim 5.3, the proof of Theorem 5.1 is thus reduced to proving Fourier tail bounds of the structured depth-22 QAC0 circuits, which we denote C′′C^{\prime\prime}, with layer-11 gates each depending on at most one input qubit (and potentially many ancillae). Specifically, it remains to prove that for any such circuit C′′C^{\prime\prime}, 𝖶≥k​[fC′′]≤ε/4{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime\prime}}]\leq\varepsilon/4 for k=Θ⁡(log⁡(1/ε))k=\Theta(\log(1/\eps)).

While the circuit C′′C^{\prime\prime} depends only on the variables in JJ that were kept alive, it will be convenient to think of it as a circuit with nn input qubits as well, where qubits outside JJ are ignored. Without loss of generality, since the computation is single-output, we only need to consider the single layer-2 gate, gg, containing the target qubit. Also, since the ancilla starting state is allowed to be an arbitrary separable state, without loss of generality, the gate gg is a CZ gate which flips the phase iff the input is |1m⟩\ket{1^{m}}, where mm is the number of input qubits to gg.

We partition the input qubits of gg into disjoint sets Q0,Q1,Q2,…,QnQ_{0},Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{n} where for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, QiQ_{i} is a set, potentially empty, of the qubits involved with the layer-1 gate containing xix_{i} and Q0Q_{0} contains the qubits coming from ancilla-only layer-1 gates. Note that for any fixed input x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the states for these different subsets are separable.

We will now impose that the input to the layer-2 gate gg is a mixed state. Specifically, any layer-1 qubit which is not contained in gg will be traced out. Let ρ0\rho_{0} be the mixed state of qubits in Q0Q_{0}. For i∈[n]i\in[n], let ρib\rho_{i}^{b} be the mixed state of the qubits in QiQ_{i} when xi=bx_{i}=b, for b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. (If Qi=∅Q_{i}=\emptyset then ρib=(1)\rho_{i}^{b}=(1), the trivial mixed state of dimension one, for both b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.) Then, on input x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the state entering gg is

ρx=ρ0⊗ρ1x1⊗⋯⊗ρnxn.\displaystyle\rho^{x}=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}^{x_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n}^{x_{n}}. (67)

We will denote the average state over the two options for xix_{i} as

ρi=12​(ρi0+ρi1)\displaystyle\rho_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(\rho_{i}^{0}+\rho_{i}^{1}) (68)

and the average state over all 2n2^{n} options for xx as ρ\rho, where we note that

ρ=ρ0⊗ρ1⊗⋯⊗ρn.\displaystyle\rho=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n}. (69)

We will divide the remainder of the proof into two main cases. First, we consider the case in which the layer-22 gate is almost always inactive, meaning gg can be replaced by identity without notably affecting the acceptance probability on most inputs. In this case, the resultant function is close to a dictator function (i.e. depends only on one input qubit) and has extremely small Fourier tails. In the second remaining case, we argue that the “entropy” of the incoming state to the gate is small. This turns out to imply that the function’s total influence and Fourier tails are small.

Case 1: gg is almost always inactive.

Suppose ⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩≤ε/32\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32. For each fixed xx, let εx:=⟨1m|​ρx​|1m⟩\varepsilon_{x}:=\bra{1^{m}}\rho^{x}\ket{1^{m}}. Then, 𝐄x[εx]=⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩≤ε/32\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x}[\varepsilon_{x}]=\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\leq\varepsilon/32 and for each fixed xx, Lemma 5.4 implies that TD⁡(ρx,CZm⋅ρx⋅CZm)≤2​εx\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{x},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho^{x}\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})\leq 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_{x}}.

Lemma 5.4.

Let ρ\rho be a quantum mixed state on mm qubits, and let δ=⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩\delta=\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}. Then,

TD⁡(ρ,CZm⋅ρ⋅CZm)≤2​δ.\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})\leq 2\sqrt{\delta}. (70)

Therefore, removing the CZ gate, barely changes the circuit functionality. More formally, denote by C′′′C^{\prime\prime\prime} the circuit C′′C^{\prime\prime} with gate gg replaced with identity. Then,

‖fC′′−fC′′′‖22\displaystyle\|f_{C^{\prime\prime}}-f_{C^{\prime\prime\prime}}\|_{2}^{2} =𝐄x∼{0,1}n[(fC′′​(x)−fC′′′​(x))2]\displaystyle=\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[(f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x)-f_{C^{\prime\prime\prime}}(x))^{2}] (71)
≤𝐄x∼{0,1}n[TD​(ρx,CZm⋅ρx⋅CZm)2]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}\left[\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{x},\texttt{CZ}_{m}\cdot\rho^{x}\cdot\texttt{CZ}_{m})^{2}\right] (72)
≤𝐄x∼{0,1}n[εx]\displaystyle\leq\mathop{\bf E\/}_{x\sim{\{0,1\}}^{n}}[\varepsilon_{x}] (73)
≤ε/8.\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon/8. (74)

The circuit C′′′C^{\prime\prime\prime} (without gate gg replaced with identity) has only one layer of CZ gates, and its output depends on only a single input qubit, i.e., it computes a dictator function. Such a circuit has zero Fourier weight above level 11, let alone kk. Thus, via Lemma 5.5, our circuit C′′C^{\prime\prime} has at most ε/4\varepsilon/4 Fourier weight above level kk.

Lemma 5.5.

[Closeness in ℓ2\ell_{2} implies closeness in Fourier tails] Let f,g:{0,1}n→ℝf,g:{\{0,1\}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{R}}, with ‖f‖2,‖g‖2≤1\|f\|_{2},\|g\|_{2}\leq 1 and let k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. Then, |𝖶≥k​[f]−𝖶≥k​[g]|≤2⋅‖f−g‖22|{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]-{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[g]|\leq 2\cdot\|f-g\|_{2}^{2}

Case 2: gg is active with non-neglible probability.

Otherwise, ⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩≥ε/8\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}\geq\varepsilon/8. Using the fact that ρ=ρ0⊗ρ1⊗⋯⊗ρn\rho=\rho_{0}\otimes\rho_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\rho_{n},

⟨1m|​ρ​|1m⟩=∏i=0n⟨1|Qi||​ρi​|1|Qi|⟩≥ε/32.\displaystyle\bra{1^{m}}\rho\ket{1^{m}}=\prod_{i=0}^{n}\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\geq\varepsilon/32\;. (75)

Denoting δi=1−⟨1|Qi||​ρi​|1|Qi|⟩\delta_{i}=1-\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}, this implies that

∑i=0nδi=∑i=0n(1−⟨1|Qi||​ρi​|1|Qi|⟩)≤∑i=0nln⁡(1/⟨1|Qi||​ρi​|1|Qi|⟩)≤ln⁡(32/ε).\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}\delta_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\left(1-\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\right)\leq\sum_{i=0}^{n}1/\ln(1/\bra{1^{|Q_i|}}\rho_i \ket{1^{|Q_i|}})\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\leq\ln(32/\eps). (76)

Therefore, for most i∈[n]i\in[n], ⟨1|Qi||​ρi​|1|Qi|⟩\bra{1^{|Q_{i}|}}\rho_{i}\ket{1^{|Q_{i}|}} is rather close to 11. Also note that both

so Lemma 5.6 implies that TD⁡(ρi0,ρi1)≤8​δi\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1})\leq 8\sqrt{\delta_{i}}.

Lemma 5.6.

Let 0≤δ≤10\leq\delta\leq 1. Then, TD⁡(ρ′,ρ′′)≤2​δ+2​δ\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\rho^{\prime\prime})\leq 2\delta+2\sqrt{\delta}.

Next, we prove a Fourier tail bound for this case. We observe that

ρixi=ρi+(−1)xi⋅DiwhereDi=ρi1−ρi02\rho_{i}^{x_{i}}=\rho_{i}+(-1)^{x_{i}}\cdot D_{i}\qquad\text{where}\qquad D_{i}=\frac{\rho_{i}^{1}-\rho_{i}^{0}}{2}

is the derivative of ρixi\rho_{i}^{x_{i}} according to xix_{i}. This will allow us to write a nice “matrix Fourier decomposition” for ρ\rho and a bound on the Fourier spectrum of fC′′f_{C^{\prime\prime}}. With this notation,

ρ\displaystyle\rho =ρ0⊗(ρ1+(−1)x1⋅D1)⊗⋯⊗(ρn+(−1)xn⋅Dn)\displaystyle=\rho_{0}\otimes\bigg(\rho_{1}+(-1)^{x_{1}}\cdot D_{1}\bigg)\otimes\dots\otimes\bigg(\rho_{n}+(-1)^{x_{n}}\cdot D_{n}\bigg)
=∑R⊆[n](−1)∑i∈Rxi⋅ρ0⊗⨂i=1n[(ρi)𝟙i∉R​(Di)𝟙i∈R]\displaystyle=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\cdot\rho_{0}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}[(\rho_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\not\in R}}(D_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\in R}}]

So, we can think of the coefficient of (−1)∑i∈Rxi(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}} as the RR-Fourier coefficient of ρ\rho. That is,

ρ^​(R):=ρ0⊗⨂i=1n[(ρi)𝟙i∉R​(Di)𝟙i∈R].\widehat{\rho}(R):=\rho_{0}\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}[(\rho_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\not\in R}}(D_{i})^{{\mathbbm{1}}_{i\in R}}].

Note that the RR-Fourier coefficient in this case is a matrix (instead of a scalar in the standard case). Since all density matrices have trace-norm 1, ‖ρi‖1=1\|\rho_{i}\|_{1}=1 for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Therefore, since the trace is multiplicative with respect to tensor products,

‖ρ^​(R)‖1=∏i∈R‖Di‖1.\displaystyle\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}. (78)

Furthermore, observe that, by definition of trace distance, ‖Di‖1=TD⁡(ρi1,ρi0)\|D_{i}\|_{1}=\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{1},\rho_{i}^{0}) .

Now, fC′′​(x)f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x) is an application of a unitary UU and a projection Π\Pi on ρx\rho^{x}. As such,

fC′′​(x)=Tr⁡(Π​U​ρx​U†)\displaystyle f_{C^{\prime\prime}}(x)=\Tr(\Pi U \rho^x U^{\dagger} ) =Tr⁡(Π​U​∑R⊆[n](−1)∑i∈Rxi​ρ^​(R)​U†)=∑R⊆[n](−1)∑i∈Rxi​Tr⁡(Π​U​ρ^​(R)​U†).\displaystyle=\Tr\left(\Pi U\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\widehat{\rho}(R)U^{\dagger}\right)=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]}(-1)^{\sum_{i\in R}x_{i}}\Tr(\Pi U \widehat{\rho}(R) U^{\dagger} ).

From hereon, we will denote fC′′^​(R)=Tr⁡(Π​U​ρ^​(R)​U†)\widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)=\Tr(\Pi U \widehat{\rho}(R) U^{\dagger}). By properties of the trace norm, |fC′′^​(R)|≤‖ρ^​(R)‖1|\widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}. Thus, by Equation 78,

|fC′′^​(R)|≤‖ρ^​(R)‖1=∏i∈R‖Di‖1=∏i∈RTD⁡(ρi0,ρi1)≤∏i∈R8​δi.\displaystyle|\widehat{f_{C^{\prime\prime}}}(R)|\leq\|\widehat{\rho}(R)\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\|D_{i}\|_{1}=\prod_{i\in R}\mathrm{TD}(\rho_{i}^{0},\rho_{i}^{1})\leq\prod_{i\in R}8\sqrt{\delta_{i}}. (79)

Therefore, for any ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in{\mathbb{N}},

To obtain 𝖶≥k​[fC′′]≤ε/4{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C^{\prime\prime}}]\leq\varepsilon/4, it suffices to pick k=2​e⋅64​ln⁡(32/ε)=Θ⁡(ln⁡(1/ε))k=2e\cdot 64\ln(32/\eps)=\Theta(\ln(1/\eps)). ∎

5.2 Influence and Parity Correlation Bounds

Before proving the lemmata and claims used in the proof of Theorem 5.1, we prove three useful corollaries on the Fourier tails of fCf_{C}: (i) a bound on the tail 𝖶≥k​[fC]{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}] for kk in terms of kk and nn, (ii) a bound on the total influence of fCf_{C}, and (iii) a bound on the correlation of fCf_{C} with the PARITY function. All follow easily from Theorem 5.1.

Corollary 5.7.

Let c>1c>1 be the constant in Theorem 5.1. For level k≤2​c​log2⁡nk\leq 2c\log^{2}n, we have 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(k/log⁡n)){\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\exp(-\Omega(k/\log n)), and for level k≥2​c​log2⁡nk\geq 2c\log^{2}n, we have 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(k)){\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{k})).

Proof.

Theorem 5.1 implies that for any s≥0s\geq 0, if we want to get a Fourier tail bound of 𝖶≥k​[f]≤2−s{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f]\leq 2^{-s} it suffices to take k=c​log⁡(1/2−s)​log⁡(n/2−s)=c​s​(s+log⁡n)k=c\log(1/2^{-s})\log(n/2^{-s})=cs(s+\log n). We consider two cases separately depending on whether s≤log⁡ns\leq\log n or not. Note that s≤log⁡ns\leq\log n if and only if k≤2​c​log2⁡nk\leq 2c\log^{2}n, so we divide to cases based on this condition.

The Case k≤2​c​log2⁡nk\leq 2c\log^{2}n.

Let s=k/(2​c​log⁡n)≤log⁡ns=k/(2c\log n)\leq\log n and take ε=2−s\varepsilon=2^{-s}. We want to show that 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤ε{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon. Indeed, we know that 𝖶≥κ⁡(ε)​[fC]≤ε{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon for

κ⁡(ε)=c​log⁡(1/ε)​(log⁡(n/ε))=c​s​(log⁡n+s)≤2​c​s​log⁡n≤k.\kappa(\varepsilon)=c\log(1/\eps)(\log(n/\eps))=cs(\log n+s)\leq 2cs\log n\leq k.

By monotonicity of Fourier tails we get 𝖶≥k[fC]≤W≥κ⁡(ε)[fC]≤ε=2−k/2clogn{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq W^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon=2^{-k/2c\log n}.

The Case k≥2​c​log2⁡nk\geq 2c\log^{2}n.

Let s=k/2​c≥log⁡ns=\sqrt{k/2c}\geq\log n and take ε=2−s\varepsilon=2^{-s}. We want to show that 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤ε{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon. Indeed, we know that 𝖶≥κ⁡(ε)​[fC]≤ε{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq\varepsilon for κ⁡(ε)=c​s​(log⁡n+s)≤2​c​s2≤k\kappa(\varepsilon)=cs(\log n+s)\leq 2cs^{2}\leq k. Thus, we get 𝖶≥k​[fC]≤W≥κ⁡(ε)​[fC]≤2−k/2​c{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq W^{\geq\kappa(\varepsilon)}[f_{C}]\leq 2^{-\sqrt{k/2c}} ∎

Corollary 5.8.

𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[fC]≤O⁡(log⁡n){\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]\leq O(\log n).

Proof.

By the definition of total influence,

𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[fC]=∑S⊆[n]|S|⋅f^C​(S)2=∑k>1k⋅𝖶=k​[fC]=∑k>1𝖶≥k​[fC].\displaystyle{\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|\cdot\widehat{f}_{C}(S)^{2}=\sum_{k>1}k\cdot{\mathsf{W}}^{=k}[f_{C}]=\sum_{k>1}{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]. (80)

Corollary 5.7 shows that

𝖶≥k​[fC]≤{exp⁡(−Ω⁡(k/log⁡n)),if ​k≤2​c​log2​nexp⁡(−Ω⁡(k)),if ​k≥2​c​log2​n.\displaystyle{\mathsf{W}}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\leq\begin{cases}\exp(-\Omega(k/\log n)),&\text{if }k\leq 2c\log^{2}n\\ \exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{k})),&\text{if }k\geq 2c\log^{2}n\end{cases}. (81)

Thus, for some constants α\alpha and β\beta, the total influence can be bounded as

𝐈𝐧𝐟⁡[fC]≤∑k≤2​c​log2⁡nexp(−αk/logn)+∑k>2​c​log2⁡nexp⁡(−β​k)=O⁡(log⁡n).\displaystyle{\mathbf{Inf}}[f_{C}]\leq\sum_{k\leq 2c\log^{2}n}\exp(-\alpha k/\log n)+\sum_{k>2c\log^{2}n}\exp(-\beta\sqrt{k})=O(\log n).

∎

Corollary 5.9.

fCf_{C} is weakly correlated with PARITY, i.e. ⟨fC,χ[n]⟩≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n))\langle f_{C},\chi_{[n]}\rangle\leq\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})).

Proof.

The correlation of fCf_{C} with the PARITY function χ[n]\chi_{[n]} is

⟨fC,χ[n]⟩=∑S⊆[n]f^C​(S)⋅χ^[n]​(S)=f^C​([n])=𝖶=n​[fC].\displaystyle\langle f_{C},\chi_{[n]}\rangle=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}_{C}(S)\cdot\widehat{\chi}_{[n]}(S)=\widehat{f}_{C}([n])=\sqrt{{\mathsf{W}}^{=n}[f_{C}]}. (82)

Via Corollary 5.7, 𝖶=n​[fC]≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n)){\mathsf{W}}^{=n}[f_{C}]\leq\exp\left(-\Omega(\sqrt{n})\right) for nn large enough (as it satisfies n≥2​c​log2⁡nn\geq 2c\log^{2}n), which implies the desired result. ∎

Lemma 5.10.

Let ρ\rho be a quantum mixed state on finite domain XX. Then for each i∈Xi\in X, ⟨i|​ρ​|i⟩≥⟨i|​ρ2​|i⟩\bra{i}\rho\ket{i}\geq\bra{i}\rho^{2}\ket{i}.

Proof of Lemma 5.6.

We can assume δ<1/3\delta<1/3 without loss of generality, as TD⁡(ρ′,ρ′′)≤1≤2​δ+2​δ\mathrm{TD}(\rho^{\prime},\rho^{\prime\prime})\leq 1\leq 2\delta+2\sqrt{\delta} otherwise. By the triangle inequality (and symmetry), we have that

so there exists a jj with |αj|2≥1−δ|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\geq 1-\delta, and since δ<1/3\delta<1/3, jj is unique. This means that

|⟨ψj|1d⟩|2=|αj|2≥1−δ.|\braket{\psi_{j}|1^{d}}|^{2}=|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\geq 1-\delta.

Similarly,

1−δ≤⟨1d|​ρ​|1d⟩=∑k|αk|2​λj​k≤maxk⁡λk⋅∑k|αk|2=maxk⁡λk,1-\delta\leq\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{k}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}\lambda_{j}k\leq\max_{k}\lambda_{k}\cdot\sum_{k}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}=\max_{k}\lambda_{k}\;,

so there exists a kk with λk≥1−δ\lambda_{k}\geq 1-\delta, and since δ<1/3\delta<1/3, kk is unique.

Furthermore, we will now show that it must be the case that

j=arg⁡maxi​|αi|2=arg⁡maxi​λi=k,\displaystyle j={\arg\max}_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}={\arg\max}_{i}\lambda_{i}=k, (88)

which implies that there is a unique jj such that

1−δ≤|αj|2and1−δ≤λj.\displaystyle 1-\delta\leq|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad 1-\delta\leq\lambda_{j}.

We will prove this by contradiction. For contradiction, assume that Equation 88 is false so the above jj and kk are different. Since ∑iλi=1\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}=1 and λk≥1−δ\lambda_{k}\geq 1-\delta we get that λj≤δ\lambda_{j}\leq\delta. Using the assumption δ≤1/3\delta\leq 1/3 this implies that

⟨1d|ρ|1d⟩=∑i|αi|2λi≤|αj|2⋅δ+∑i:i≠j|αi|2=(∑i|αi|2)−(1−δ)|αj|2≤1−(1−δ)2≤5/9.\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}=\sum_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}\lambda_{i}\leq|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\cdot\delta+\sum_{i:i\neq j}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}=\left(\sum_{i}|\alpha_{i}|^{2}\right)-(1-\delta)|\alpha_{j}|^{2}\leq 1-(1-\delta)^{2}\leq 5/9.

However, this contradicts the assumption that ⟨1d|​ρ​|1d⟩≥1−δ>2/3\bra{1^{d}}\rho\ket{1^{d}}\geq 1-\delta>2/3.

Overall, we have shown that there exists an eigenvector of ρ\rho, denoted |ψj⟩\ket{\psi_{j}}, such that, by the definition of trace distance for pure states,

and, since the trace norm can be expressed as the sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues,

By triangle inequality, this therefore implies that TD⁡(ρ,|1d⟩​⟨1d|)≤δ+δ\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\outerproduct*{1^d}{1^d})\leq\delta+\sqrt{\delta}. ∎

6 Depth-2 Circuits Cannot Construct a Nekomata

We will now prove that a depth-22 QAC0 circuit cannot exactly synthesize a generalized nn-nekomata even with unlimited ancillae. We will refer to the definitions in Section 3.5.

The outline of our proof is as follows. Given a depth-dd circuit that output a nn-qubit nekomata, we will construct a separable state on some subset of qubits, |η→⟩Q\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}, such that, inside the eigenspace of |η→⟩​⟨η→|Q\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q}, (1) the state is still a nekomata and (2) the final layer is simplified to a single-qubit layer. The main idea behind this is the same as the block diagonalization used in Lemma 4.5. To complete our proof for d=2d=2, we show that a depth-11 QAC circuit cannot compute a state that looks like an Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1)-qubit nekomata, even after post-selecting for such |η→⟩​⟨η→|Q\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q} as in Definition 3.7

Then, the two main components are given by the following lemmas. {restatable*}[Nekomata after one layer]lemmanekotognsp Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a nn-nekomata. Then, for any layer LL of separable reflection gates, the state |φ⟩\ket{\varphi} given by |φ⟩=L⋅|ψ⟩\ket{\varphi}=L\cdot\ket{\psi} is an ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil-GNSP.

{restatable*}

[No GNSP in depth-11]lemmaonelayergnsp Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a state constructed by a depth-11 QAC0 circuit CC. Then, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} cannot be a nn-GNSP for any n>2n>2. Then, the bound from Theorem 1.5 immediately follows as a consequence,

Corollary 6.1.

Let |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} be a state constructed by a depth-22 QAC0 circuit CC starting from the |0→⟩\ket{{\vec{0}}} state. Then, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} cannot be a generalized nn-nekomata for n>4n>4.

Proof.

Assuming for contradiction that |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is a generalized nn-nekomata for n≥5n\geq 5. Then, letting |φ⟩\ket{\varphi} be the state after the first layer of CC, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is given by |ψ⟩=L⋅|φ⟩\ket{\psi}=L\cdot\ket{\varphi} for the second layer LL. Since all reflection gates are Hermitian, |φ⟩=L⋅|ψ⟩\ket{\varphi}=L\cdot\ket{\psi} and due to Section 6, |φ⟩\ket{\varphi} is an 33-GNSP. This is a contradiction to Section 6. ∎

6.1 Proofs of Lemmata

First, we show the following observation.

Fact 6.2.

Let |ψ⟩T,A\ket{\psi}_{T,A} be a generalized nn-nekomata on targets t1,t2​…​tnt_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n} and ancillae AA. Then, for any unitary UAU_{A} acting only on the ancillae, the state UA⋅|ψ⟩U_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi} is still a generalized nn-nekomata on targets t1,t2​…​tnt_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n}.

Proof.

Suppose |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is given by,

|ψ⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psi} =α⋅|μ1⟩t1​|μ2⟩t2​…​|μn⟩tn​|γ0⟩A+β⋅|μ1⟂⟩t1​|μ2⟂⟩t2​…​|μn⟂⟩tn​|γ1⟩A\displaystyle=\alpha\cdot\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\cdot\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu^{\perp}_{n}}_{t_{n}}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A} (91)

Then,

UA⋅|ψ⟩\displaystyle U_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi} =α​|μ1⟩t1​|μ2⟩t2​…​|μn⟩tn​UA​|γ0⟩A+β​|μ1⟂⟩t1​|μ2⟂⟩t2​…​|μn⟂⟩tn​UA​|γ1⟩A\displaystyle=\alpha\ket{\mu_{1}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}}_{t_{n}}U_{A}\ket{\gamma_{0}}_{A}+\beta\ket{\mu_{1}^{\perp}}_{t_{1}}\ket{\mu_{2}^{\perp}}_{t_{2}}\dots\ket{\mu_{n}^{\perp}}_{t_{n}}U_{A}\ket{\gamma_{1}}_{A} (92)

which is also a generalized nn-nekomata on the same targets. ∎

Now we provide the proofs of the lemmas. First, we will prove a special case of Section 6 for a single gate.

For m>1m>1, let G⁡(S)=(I−2​|θ→⟩​⟨θ→|S)G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) be a gate in LL so that L=G⁡(S)⊗L1L=G(S)\otimes L_{1}, where L1L_{1} contains m−1m-1 gates and let n1n_{1} be the number of targets from TT in L1L_{1} and n2=n0−n1n_{2}=n_{0}-n_{1} be the number of targets in SS. Then, from the inductive hypothesis on |φ1⟩=L1⋅|ψ⟩\ket{\varphi_{1}}=L_{1}\cdot\ket{\psi}, there is a state |η→⟩Q1\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{1}} only on qubits in L1L_{1} such that the state |ψ1⟩∝|η→⟩​⟨η→|Q1⋅|φ1⟩\ket{\psi_{1}}\propto\outerproduct*{\veta}{\veta}_{Q_{1}}\cdot\ket{\varphi_{1}} is a generalized n−⌊n1/2⌋n-\lfloor n_{1}/2\rfloor-nekomata. ≥n−⌊n0/2⌋\displaystyle\geq n-\lfloor n_{0}/2\rfloor (105)

Then, for Q=Q1∪Q2⊆Q0Q=Q_{1}\cup Q_{2}\subseteq Q_{0} and |η→⟩Q=|η→⟩Q1⊗|η→⟩Q2\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q}=\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{1}}\otimes\ket{\vec{\eta}}_{Q_{2}},

∝|ψ2⟩\displaystyle\propto\ket{\psi_{2}} (109)

Note that |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is separable across S1,S2​…​SmS_{1},S_{2}\dots S_{m}, the subset of qubits belonging to each of the mm gates of CC. Therefore, it suffices to prove the lemma for when CC consisting of a single gate. Then, |ψ⟩=(I−2​|θ→1⟩​⟨θ→1|S)⋅|θ→0⟩S\ket{\psi}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth^1}{\vth^1}_{S})\cdot\ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}}_{S} for separable states |θ→0⟩,|θ→1⟩\ket{\vec{\theta}^{0}},\ket{\vec{\theta}^{1}} such that 0<|⟨θq1|θq0⟩|<10<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{1}_{q}|\theta^{0}_{q}}\right\rvert<1 for every q∈Sq\in S. for some α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and β≠0\beta\neq 0 such that S′=T∪AS^{\prime}=T\cup A. For any target t∈Tt\in T, since 0<|⟨θt0|θt1⟩|<10<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{0}_{t}|\theta^{1}_{t}}\right\rvert<1 there must be some b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} for which 0<|⟨θtb|0⟩|<10<\left\lvert\braket{\theta^{b}_{t}|0}\right\rvert<1.
